## business-model / 06_value-chain.md

_Source: `business-model/06_value-chain.md`_

# Value Chain Position — ORCL

## 1. Stages Occupied

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Component/capacity buyer & cloud-infrastructure (IaaS) platform | Oracle buys GPUs, memory, servers and power, builds and operates data centers, and rents the resulting compute/storage/networking capacity (OCI) mainly to AI-model builders and enterprises [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.1-4]. | Weak | Mid | "We do rely on sole and/or single sources for certain hardware components" [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.3952]; "industry supply capacity for AI accelerators, including graphics processing units, as well as memory devices, is competitive, and we at times have to accept less favorable terms with suppliers to minimize supply constraints" [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.5907]; against that, "our global GPU utilization rate is 97.5%," and returned capacity is "instantly snapped up" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Magouyrk]; but the largest deals show customer leverage too — "$75 billion" of RPO is bring-your-own-hardware or prepaid (i.e., the customer, not Oracle, supplies or funds part of the input) and "4 customers contract[ed] for more than $8 billion this quarter" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Magouyrk] |
| End-customer-facing brand — Cloud Applications (SaaS) and on-premise Database/software (license + support) | Oracle sells proprietary enterprise software — Fusion, NetSuite, Oracle Database — directly to businesses/governments and indirectly through the Oracle Partner Network reseller channel [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.2]. | Strong | Mid | Software is internally developed IP with no meaningful third-party input dependency (upstream power = Strong by default). Downstream: FY2026 software (license + support) revenue was $24.5 billion, down 1%, "as customers migrate to cloud" [Q4FY26 Earnings Press Release, p.1; FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.2], and management is actively rolling out new "outcome-based" and token-bundle pricing because customers are asking "how much are we going to spend on AI?" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Sicilia] — evidence of real customer price sensitivity, not unchecked pricing power |
| Manufacturer/processor — Hardware (Engineered Systems, servers, storage) | Oracle designs proprietary server/storage systems but outsources most manufacturing and assembly to third parties, then sells the hardware plus support [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.2]. | Weak | Mid | "We outsource most of our manufacturing, assembly, delivery and technology of, and certain component designs for, our hardware products to a variety of companies, many of which are located outside the U.S. From time to time, these partners experience production problems or delays" [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.5912]. Downstream: FY2026 hardware revenue was $3.1 billion (5% of total), up 5% [Q4FY26 Earnings Press Release, p.1] — a small, largely captive add-on for existing Oracle Database customers, not a business with broad pricing leverage |
| Service provider — Consulting/professional services | Billed consulting and customer-success engagements, generally lower-margin than the other three businesses [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.2]. | N/A | Weak | FY2026 services revenue was $5.7 billion (8% of total), up 10% [Q4FY26 Earnings Press Release, p.1]; business-identity flags this as "generally lower-margin than the other businesses" [02_business-identity.md §2] — labor/hours-billed consulting is a price-taking category against enterprise buying departments, with no disclosed pricing-power evidence in this pool |

Bargaining power bands:
- **Strong:** Company sets price, dictates terms, has alternatives
- **Mid:** Negotiated outcomes, no extreme leverage either way
- **Weak:** Price-taker, terms imposed, few alternatives

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

Oracle's pass-through mechanism is structural and forward-looking, not retroactive, and it runs through contract design rather than list-price increases. CEO Clay Magouyrk described it directly on the Q4 FY26 call: "When we're selling stuff at a time period where we have certainty... whether it be space and power costs, energy costs, people costs, component costs... we will then do fixed-price contracts. At times that we don't know those costs because it's out too far in the future or we have too much supply chain risk... we then do not do fixed-price contracts with our customers and we have a mechanism whereby those costs end up being floating" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Magouyrk]. In plain terms: on new, uncertain-cost contracts Oracle indexes price to its own input costs (a real pass-through clause); on contracts already locked at a fixed price, a subsequent rise in memory, SSD or GPU costs is absorbed by Oracle, not passed on — the analyst who raised the question noted "component costs have gone up a lot, especially memory" [Q4 FY26 transcript, John DiFucci, Guggenheim]. This lag shows up at the margin line: management flagged a roughly 5-point full-year gross-margin step-down in FY2026 and guided to a further FY2027 step-down "due to timing for the ramp-up of our data center projects into their full revenue contribution plus impacts from mix" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CFO Maxson] — i.e., new capacity is expensed as it comes online but takes time to earn its full contracted revenue, so input-cost absorption runs ahead of pass-through in the near term. On the legacy software side, support renewals reprice roughly annually as a percentage of the original license fee, but the filings disclose no explicit CPI-linked or indexed escalator clause — pricing there is set by Oracle's own list price and discounting practice, not a contractual pass-through mechanism [02_business-identity.md §2].

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** The 10-K discloses only qualitative concentration language — "we do rely on sole and/or single sources for certain hardware components" [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.3952] — and does not disclose a percentage of COGS or capital spend tied to any single supplier. NVIDIA Corporation is named as a supplier in the CIQ relationship data (Semiconductors) [Oracle-Corporation-NYSE-ORCL-Suppliers.txt], and Oracle's own disclosures describe its largest AI clusters as built on "hundreds of thousands of NVIDIA GPUs" [10_external-dependency.md, citing Key Developments 2025-10-14]. Given that GPU accelerators are the single largest driver of the AI-infrastructure capex program (net capex outlay of roughly $48 billion in FY2026, guided to ~$70 billion in FY2027 [Q4 FY26 transcript, CFO Maxson]), NVIDIA is very likely Oracle's largest single hardware-related dependency by dollar value — but this is **Inference, not from filings**: no filing states a specific percentage, and downstream agents should not invent one. What the filings do state is a genuine, named risk: memory and SSD suppliers are also named as a source of recent cost inflation [Q4 FY26 transcript, John DiFucci], and Oracle "at times has to accept less favorable terms with suppliers to minimize supply constraints" [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.5907] — a disclosed, material single-input dependency that is a genuine bargaining risk carried into §5 below.

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

Oracle currently shows real, if concentrated and unquantified, pricing power on the OCI side: global GPU utilization is 97.5%, and in the most recent quarter "35,000 GPUs from 59 separate customers were up for renewal. 49% of those customers renewed for 92% of those GPUs" with the remainder "subsequently sold to other customers in the same quarter" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Magouyrk] — a supply-constrained market in which Oracle is not chasing volume with discounts. Management also introduced new monetization layers in Q4 FY26 — outcome-based pricing and token bundles — with "33 customers... repurchase[d] tokens to have access to more advanced reasoning and models" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Sicilia], but this is a 33-customer early rollout, not a disclosed broad-based price increase with a measured volume reaction; treat it as **Not proven from available data** as an economy-wide pricing action. On the legacy license/support book, the opposite signal holds: software revenue fell 1% in FY2026 "as customers migrate to cloud" [Q4FY26 Earnings Press Release, p.1], which is evidence of customers voting with their feet rather than Oracle successfully raising price without losing volume. No explicit "we raised price X%, volume moved Y%" disclosure exists anywhere in this data pool for either business — that comparison is **Not proven from available data**.

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.** Oracle is a price-taker on the physical inputs that now drive its growth — sole/single-sourced GPU, memory and component vendors, and a global power market it does not control, where the company itself says it "accept[s] less favorable terms with suppliers to minimize supply constraints" [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.5907]. On the customer side it currently holds real leverage in its fastest-growing business (OCI, 97.5% utilization, capacity "instantly snapped up") and a sticky, high-switching-cost legacy database franchise, but that leverage is concentrated in a small number of very large AI-infrastructure counterparties (four customers over $8 billion each in a single quarter) who have visible alternatives entering the market (competing hyperscalers, "NeoCloud, SpaceX" building their own data centers, per the Bernstein analyst's own framing on the call) [Q4 FY26 transcript, Mark Moerdler, Bernstein].

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

The GPU/power supply relationship sitting upstream of OCI: Oracle has already disclosed that it accepts worse terms from sole/single-source chip and component vendors to keep AI-infrastructure supply flowing [FY26 10-K, Item 1, p.5907], and if that squeeze tightens further (NVIDIA allocation shifting toward its own cloud or larger hyperscalers, continued memory/SSD cost inflation, or power-supply constraints — "constrained globally" per the 10-K's own risk factors [10_external-dependency.md]) it would compress margins on the very backlog ($638 billion of RPO) that the market is now pricing Oracle on, before Oracle's downstream pricing power over its concentrated set of AI-infrastructure customers has a chance to offset it.

## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

_Source: `business-model/07_business-quality.md`_

# Business Quality — ORCL

Upstream inputs used: `02_business-identity.md`, `03_segment-map.md`, `05_customer-geography.md` — all three present and complete. No degraded-confidence flag required.

**Sector overlay applied:** Oracle is classified as a hybrid enterprise-software/cloud-infrastructure company that maps closest to the **SaaS / subscription software** row in `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md` [`02_business-identity.md`, §3a]. Per the overlay: **recurring revenue** is scored on RPO/cRPO and support-renewal visibility rather than a generic "repeat sales" read; **margin stability** is scored on GAAP gross margin (not non-GAAP, which masks the widening stock-based-compensation gap); **capital intensity** is NOT treated as automatically low the way a pure-play SaaS company would be — Oracle's cloud-infrastructure (OCI) build-out is genuinely capital-heavy (data-center leases, chips, power), so this factor uses the actual capex/revenue and free-cash-flow data rather than a software-default assumption.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 55 | Software support renews at a fixed percentage of the original license fee on a large, sticky installed base — support revenue was $19,804M in FY26, +1% y/y, essentially flat despite the license base shrinking (license revenue -9%) [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, "Revenues by Offerings," p.45]. But the 10-K states plainly: "If our competitors offer deep discounts on certain products or services... we may need to lower prices... Our competitors may offer lower pricing on their support offerings, which could put pressure on us to further discount" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5994] | Pricing power is real but asymmetric — strong in the legacy support annuity, contested in cloud infrastructure where OCI prices against hyperscalers on a largely commoditized compute/storage basis |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better)* | 75 | Total Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) — the forward, contracted-but-unrecognized order book — was $638 billion at FYE26, up 363% y/y from $138 billion; management disclosed ~12% (~$76.6bn) recognizing in the next 12 months and 34% in months 13-36 [`02_business-identity.md` §2; FY26 10-K, Note 1/MD&A p.22]. Cloud revenue (applications + infrastructure) reached 51% of total revenue in FY26, up from 43% in FY25 [`03_segment-map.md` §1]. Software support (~30% of total revenue) renews annually and is the most predictable line in the business | Strong and improving forward visibility, but a large share of the RPO increase is prepaid or customer-supplied-hardware AI infrastructure contracts, a different risk profile from software-subscription bookings [`02_business-identity.md` §3a] — and no disclosed net-retention or billings figure exists to confirm underlying subscription health independent of a handful of AI mega-deals |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 62 | Mission-critical databases and ERP systems are costly and risky to replace — the installed base underpins the stable support-renewal annuity. No single customer is >10% of *recognized* revenue in FY26, FY25 or FY24 [`05_customer-geography.md` §1; FY26 10-K, Note 1] | Stickiness in the legacy core is high, but the fastest-growing part of the business (OCI/AI infrastructure) is a newer relationship set concentrated among a small number of large, recently-signed customers (AMD, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, TikTok, xAI) whose durability over a full cycle is unproven — "we are more concentrated among a number of large customers, which could increase these risks [of non-payment/non-performance]" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A; `05_customer-geography.md` §1] |
| Margin stability *(higher = better)* | 30 | GAAP gross margin has fallen every year for five straight years: 80.6% (FY21) → 79.1% (FY22) → 72.8% (FY23) → 71.4% (FY24) → 70.5% (FY25) → 65.8% (FY26) [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab, FY2017-FY2026]. Management flagged a further ~5-point full-year gross-margin step-down in FY2026 specifically from data-center ramp-up [`02_business-identity.md` §2; Q4 FY26 earnings call, CFO Hilary Maxson prepared remarks] | A ~15-point structural gross-margin decline over five years is a material stability problem, not noise — it is the direct, disclosed consequence of building OCI capacity ahead of the revenue it earns |
| Capital intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 12 | Capital expenditure exploded from $6,866M (FY24) to $21,215M (FY25) to $55,663M (FY26) on the CIQ cash-flow basis [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, FY2017-FY2026] — 82.6% of FY26 revenue ($55,663M/$67,357M). Management's own investor-deck figure (net cash capex, a narrower basis) was $48 billion in FY26, guided to ~$70 billion in FY27 [`03_segment-map.md` §1; Q4 FY26 investor deck, slide 15] — both figures are shown because they use different bases and should not be netted together. Levered free cash flow margin swung from +19.7% (FY24) to +1.2% (FY25) to **-36.4%** (FY26) [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab] | This is now one of the most capital-intensive businesses of its size in the S&P 500 — capex/revenue in the 70-80%+ range and negative free cash flow are far outside any software-company norm and are the dominant fact about this business today |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 27 | "We face intense competition in all aspects of our business... due to the low barriers to entry in many of our market segments, new technologies and new and growing competitors frequently emerge" — named directly against Adobe, Alphabet, Amazon, Cisco, Intel, IBM, Microsoft, Salesforce and SAP, plus Cerner-era healthcare-IT competitors [FY26 10-K, Item 1, "Competition," p.11] | The competitive set in the fastest-growing segment (OCI) is the best-capitalized group of companies in the world (Amazon/AWS, Microsoft/Azure, Google Cloud) — Oracle is a share-gainer today on the strength of its order book, but it is not competing from a position of structural insulation in that segment |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 33 | Oracle's growth is now overwhelmingly AI-infrastructure-driven: OCI revenue +77% for FY26 and +93% in Q4 alone, funded by a capex program that assumes multi-year demand for GPU-based compute that did not exist at scale three years ago [`02_business-identity.md` §4; `03_segment-map.md` §1]. The 10-K itself flags: "Machine learning and AI... are highly competitive and rapidly evolving" and cites an evolving, still-being-written regulatory framework (EU AI Act phasing in through 2030, a "patchwork" of US state/federal rules) [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5708, ~5767] | The AI-infrastructure buildout that now drives nearly all of Oracle's incremental revenue and capex is a technology and demand cycle whose long-run winners, useful life of GPU-era assets, and durable unit economics are not yet established — this is the Filter-5 (CLAUDE.md §24) condition, scored accordingly |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 50 | Material but diffuse regulatory exposure: data privacy/GDPR (fines up to the greater of €20M or 4% of worldwide revenue), an evolving AI-specific regulatory patchwork (EU AI Act, US state/federal), export controls and sanctions relevant to GPU/chip supply, healthcare-industry regulation from the Cerner acquisition, and government-customer contracts "terminable... at its convenience" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~6462-6519, ~5767, ~5392; `05_customer-geography.md` §1] | Not a price-regulated utility, but the AI-compute business specifically sits inside a still-forming regulatory perimeter (export controls on chips, emerging AI law) that did not exist for Oracle's legacy database/ERP business |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 45 | Oracle does not sell a commodity, but its capital-intensive OCI build-out is dependent on GPU supply, power, and single-sourced hardware components: "there are some technologies and components that can only be purchased from a single vendor" and supply is exposed to "industry consolidation and component constraints or shortages... political unrest... tensions between China and Taiwan" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5902] | The dependence is on critical inputs (GPUs, power, chips) rather than a sold commodity, but it is a real and newly material constraint on the fastest-growing part of the business, so this scores below the generic-software default |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 38 | Legacy software support was historically low-cyclicality (renewal-based); Services is explicitly flagged as the most cyclical segment, tied to "personnel reductions in our customers' IT departments" and "tighter controls over customer discretionary spending" [`03_segment-map.md` §1]. The now-dominant growth driver is lumpy: management cited four customers each contracting for more than $8 billion in a single quarter [`02_business-identity.md` §4] | The blended cyclicality profile is shifting from a low-cyclicality software annuity toward a lumpier, large-contract-driven infrastructure business funded by rising leverage (Net Debt/EBITDA 4.07x FY26 vs 3.63x FY24) [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab] — a downturn in AI-infrastructure demand would hit a business now carrying a much larger fixed-cost and debt base than three years ago |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 62 | Audited 10-K/10-Q SEC filer with a detailed segment note, GAAP-to-non-GAAP EPS reconciliation ($5.83 GAAP vs $7.63 non-GAAP FY26), full geographic revenue and long-lived-asset breakdown, and RPO disclosure [`02_business-identity.md` §3a; `05_customer-geography.md` §2]. Segment "Margin" excludes R&D, G&A, stock-based comp and amortization — a disclosed but non-GAAP construct [`03_segment-map.md` §3] | Real gaps for a company this reliant on AI-infrastructure contracts: no net-retention/billings disclosure, no segment-level assets or capex, and the ~$300B OpenAI/Stargate contract size is not itemized anywhere in the audited filing — the RPO concentration that matters most to the thesis has to be triangulated from non-filing sources [`05_customer-geography.md` §1, §4] |

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**Aggregate: 43/100 (Mixed/Average, lower half of the band).**

Row scores sorted ascending: Capital intensity 12, Competitive intensity 27, Margin stability 30, Rate-of-change 33, Cyclicality 38, Commodity dependence 45, Regulatory dependence 50, Pricing power 55, Customer stickiness 62, Disclosure quality 62, Recurring revenue 75. The second-lowest row is Competitive intensity at 27, so the band anchor caps the aggregate at 27+20 = 47; 43 sits inside that ceiling. It is also inside the module's own rate-of-change cap (Business Quality aggregate max 65 when the disruption-risk row scores ≤40 [`MODULE_RULES.md`, Rejector-Filter table]) — the more restrictive of the two caps (47) governs.

The weighting is explicitly **not** a simple average. Capital intensity, margin stability, competitive intensity and rate-of-change together carry roughly 55% of the judgment weight because they describe the part of the business now generating essentially all of the incremental revenue and all of the capital spend (OCI/AI infrastructure) — a segment that is capital-heavy, margin-dilutive, contested by the best-funded competitors on earth, and technologically unsettled. Recurring revenue and customer stickiness carry about 25% of the weight, reflecting the genuine, filing-proven annuity quality of the legacy software-support base. Pricing power, regulatory dependence, commodity dependence and disclosure quality carry the remaining 20% as secondary factors. The result is a business quality profile pulled down hard by what is now the dominant, not the peripheral, part of the company.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Recurring / repeat revenue | 75 | $638B RPO order book (+363% y/y) and a software-support base renewing at ~flat revenue despite a shrinking license base give real forward visibility, even though the RPO's AI-contract composition is not itemized in the filing [`02_business-identity.md` §2] |
| Weakest | Capital intensity | 12 | Capex/revenue of roughly 70-83% depending on basis, and levered free cash flow that swung from +19.7% margin (FY24) to -36.4% margin (FY26), are structurally outside any comparable software company's profile [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios/Cash Flow tabs] |

## 4. Read

Oracle today is two businesses inside one income statement: a durable, high-margin, low-capital-intensity software-support annuity (the historical compounder) bolted onto a fast-growing, capital-devouring, competitively contested AI-infrastructure business (OCI) that is now the entire growth story. The legacy piece still scores well on recurring revenue and stickiness, but it is shrinking as a share of the whole (software license revenue -9% y/y), and the piece actually driving results — OCI, at +77% for the year and +93% in Q4 — is the one dragging gross margin down five straight years to 65.8% [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab] and consuming capex equal to roughly three-quarters of total revenue. Return on capital is not sitting at a cyclical peak that a buyer should discount for mean reversion — it has actually been declining (Return on Capital % fell from 12.3% in FY22 to 8.2% in FY26 [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab]) even as revenue growth accelerated, because the capex base is growing faster than the earnings it has not yet produced; the two facts (headline revenue acceleration and declining returns on capital) reconcile as the same underlying story — a business in the early, unproven-payback phase of an infrastructure build, not a business enjoying a temporary margin high. The single quality factor a buyer should watch over the next 24 months is **capital intensity converting into free-cash-flow recovery** — specifically whether the ~$638B RPO book actually converts to recognized, cash-generative revenue on schedule as the FY27 ~$70B capex program comes online, or whether demand growth decelerates while the depreciation and lease commitments remain fixed.

Because the industry rate-of-change / disruption-risk row scored 33 (≤40), this reads closer to a sector / technology-cycle bet on AI infrastructure demand than a durable software compounder for the portion of the business now driving results (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 5) — the legacy database/ERP annuity is durable, but it is no longer what determines the outcome of an Oracle investment over the next two years.

RF-BQ-005 (fast-changing industry: rate-of-change ≤40)

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — ORCL

Both required upstream inputs are present: `02_business-identity.md` and `03_segment-map.md`.

## 1. Dominant Segment

Cloud and Software is the dominant segment — 86.9% of FY2026 revenue ($58,530M of $67,357M) and 90.7% of FY2026 total segment margin — and within it, cloud infrastructure (OCI) is the fastest-growing and most capital-intensive piece, up 77% to $18.1 billion in FY2026 [FY26 10-K, Note 13, p.100; segment-map upstream, Section 2].

## 2. Named Competitors

Oracle's own FY26 10-K Risk Factors name its competitive set directly: "Adobe Systems Incorporated, Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com, Inc., Cisco Systems, Inc., Intel Corporation, International Business Machines Corporation, Microsoft Corporation, Salesforce, Inc. and SAP SE, as well as other companies like Hewlett-Packard Enterprise and Workday, Inc." [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~4]. A separate risk-factor passage on Oracle's multicloud strategy names the three hyperscale infrastructure rivals specifically: "OCI's multicloud services work with a number of our competitors' products, including Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5 area]. From this named set, the three profiled below were selected because they are of comparable or larger scale, are named directly in the 10-K, and span the two halves of the dominant segment that matter most (cloud infrastructure and cloud/on-premise applications): Microsoft (both infrastructure and applications), Amazon (pure infrastructure, AWS), and SAP (applications/ERP, the closest direct rival to Oracle Fusion and NetSuite).

### Competitor A — Microsoft Corporation

- **Ticker / listing:** NasdaqGS:MSFT
- **Where they compete:** Cloud infrastructure via Azure (direct OCI rival, explicitly named alongside AWS and Google Cloud in Oracle's multicloud risk factor) and cloud/on-premise applications via Dynamics 365 (rival to Oracle Fusion/NetSuite) [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~4-5].
- **Scale:** Total company revenue $331.8 billion for fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, up 18% [Web: Microsoft FY26 Q4 press release/10-K coverage, 2026-07-29 (unverified, dated)]. Intelligent Cloud segment (which houses Azure) revenue was $39.3 billion in the June-2026 quarter alone, up 32% (31% constant currency), with Azure and other cloud services revenue up 43% [Web: Microsoft FY26 Q4 investor materials, 2026-07-29 (unverified, dated)]. This is roughly 4.9x Oracle's FY2026 total revenue of $67.4 billion [Q4FY26 Earnings Press Release, p.1].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM EBIT margin 46.8%, LTM EBITDA margin 58.5%, LTM net income margin 40.3% [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-08-13] — versus Oracle's own LTM EBIT margin of 33.2% and LTM net income margin of 25.4% in the same comp set [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-08-13]. Company-wide operating margin (not Azure-specific) was reported at roughly 45% in the June-2026 quarter [Web: Microsoft FY26 Q4 coverage, 2026-07-29 (unverified, dated)]. ROIC/ROE not independently computed here — not in the CIQ comp export pulled; flagged as a gap for the `moat` agent to fill if needed.
- **Source named in:** [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~4-5 (both the broad competitor list and the Azure-specific multicloud passage)]
- **One-line read:** Larger, more profitable, and diversified across infrastructure and applications — Microsoft is the single most direct, comparable-scale rival across both halves of Oracle's dominant segment.

### Competitor B — Amazon.com, Inc. (AWS segment)

- **Ticker / listing:** NasdaqGS:AMZN
- **Where they compete:** Cloud infrastructure only, via Amazon Web Services (AWS) — the direct rival to OCI, explicitly named in Oracle's multicloud risk factor [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5 area].
- **Scale:** AWS segment sales were $128.7 billion for full-year 2025, up 20% year over year [Web: Amazon FY2025 10-K/annual report coverage, 2026 (unverified, dated)] — about 7.1x Oracle's FY2026 cloud infrastructure revenue of $18.1 billion [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, "Revenues by Offerings," p.45]. In the most recent reported quarter (Q2 2026, calendar), AWS revenue was $42.2 billion, up 36.7% year over year [Web: Amazon Q2 2026 earnings coverage, 2026-07-30 (unverified, dated)].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** AWS segment operating income was $45.6 billion on $128.7 billion of revenue in full-year 2025, an operating margin of about 35.4% [Web: Amazon FY2025 10-K/annual report coverage, 2026 (unverified, dated) — margin is this agent's calculation from the two disclosed figures]. In Q2 2026 the AWS operating margin expanded to 39.4% (operating income $16.6 billion on $42.2 billion revenue), up roughly 650 basis points year over year [Web: Amazon Q2 2026 earnings coverage, 2026-07-30 (unverified, dated)]. Amazon-consolidated ROIC/ROE not pulled — not evaluated here; AWS-specific return on capital is not separately disclosed by Amazon.
- **Source named in:** [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~4-5]
- **One-line read:** AWS is the largest hyperscaler by revenue and runs a materially higher, and improving, operating margin than Oracle's consolidated business — a pure infrastructure comparison that is the toughest read on OCI's unit economics once OCI reaches AWS's scale.

### Competitor C — SAP SE

- **Ticker / listing:** XTRA:SAP (ADR: NYSE:SAP)
- **Where they compete:** Cloud and on-premise enterprise applications (ERP, finance, supply chain) — the direct rival to Oracle Fusion and NetSuite within the applications half of the Cloud and Software segment [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~4].
- **Scale:** Cloud revenue of €6.3 billion in Q2 2026, up 22% (24% constant currency); current cloud backlog €22.9 billion, up 27% [Web: SAP Q2 2026 quarterly statement, 2026-07-23 (unverified, dated)]. Company-wide LTM revenue growth of 6.4% per the Capital IQ comp set [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-08-13] — a smaller and slower-growing company than Oracle at the consolidated level, though its cloud applications line competes head-on with Oracle's SaaS applications revenue of $15.9 billion (+11%) [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, "Revenues by Offerings," p.45].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM EBIT margin 28.8%, LTM EBITDA margin 30.8%, LTM net income margin 20.4% [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-08-13] — below Oracle's LTM EBIT margin of 33.2% in the same comp set. Non-IFRS cloud gross margin was 74.6% in Q2 2026, down 0.7 points year over year on AI-investment and acquisition costs [Web: SAP Q2 2026 quarterly statement, 2026-07-23 (unverified, dated)]. ROIC/ROE not pulled from this data set — flagged as a gap.
- **Source named in:** [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~4]
- **One-line read:** SAP is the applications-layer peer where Oracle currently earns a higher company-level margin, but SAP's cloud backlog growth (27%) is outpacing Oracle's total cloud applications growth (11%), suggesting SAP is not losing ground in ERP despite its lower overall margin.

## 3. Competitive Position

Oracle's position varies sharply by sub-market. In cloud infrastructure, Oracle holds roughly 3% of global cloud infrastructure spending versus AWS's 28%, Azure's 21%, and Google Cloud's 14% [Web: Synergy Research Group, cloud market share commentary, 2026 (unverified, dated)] — a small base, but Oracle's reported infrastructure growth (77% FY2026, 93% in Q4 alone) and its 363% RPO surge to $638 billion outpace AWS's 20-37% and sit closer to Google Cloud's fastest-in-class 63% [Q4FY26 Earnings Press Release, p.1-2; Web: Synergy Research Group, 2026 (unverified, dated)]. This is best read as **gaining share off a small base**, not holding or losing — but the RPO figure itself is a proxy for future, not realized, revenue, and $75 billion of the RPO increase is prepaid or customer-supplied-hardware contracts, a different risk profile from steady-state infrastructure revenue [FY26 10-K, Note 1 area; business-identity upstream, Section 3a]. In cloud applications, Oracle's 11% SaaS growth trails SAP's 22-27% cloud/backlog growth, which reads as **holding at best, more likely losing relative share** in the applications sub-market, though no head-count or seat-share data is disclosed by either company to confirm this directly. No official market-share disclosure exists from Oracle itself in this pool; the reads above rely on the third-party Synergy Research proxy and on relative growth-rate comparisons, both labelled and dated.

## 4. Competitive Shape

Cloud infrastructure (OCI's market) is an **oligopoly**: the "Big Three" (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) together hold 63% of a $129 billion-per-quarter global market, with Oracle and a set of smaller "neoclouds" splitting a low-single-digit-percent remainder [Web: Synergy Research Group, cloud market share commentary, 2026 (unverified, dated)]. Cloud/on-premise enterprise applications (Oracle Fusion, NetSuite vs. SAP, Salesforce, Workday, Microsoft Dynamics) is more **fragmented at the margin but consolidated at the top** — a handful of large vendors (SAP, Oracle, Microsoft, Salesforce, Workday) dominate large-enterprise ERP and CRM, each named directly as a competitor in Oracle's own risk factors, with lower barriers to entry in narrower point-solution niches, per Oracle's own description: "due to the low barriers to entry in many of our market segments, new technologies and new and growing competitors frequently emerge" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~4].

## 5. Caveat

Two gaps to flag. First, ROIC/ROE figures for Microsoft, Amazon, and SAP were not available in the Capital IQ comp export pulled for this report (which carried margin and multiple data but not return-on-capital ratios); the `moat` agent should pull these separately if a capital-efficiency comparison beyond operating margin is required — do not infer them from the margin data above. Second, several of the peer figures above (Microsoft's segment detail, AWS's full-year 2025 and Q2-2026 figures, SAP's Q2 2026 cloud metrics) come from web-search coverage of each company's own results rather than this data pool's filings, since none of the three peers' 10-Ks/annual reports are in `data/ORCL/`. These are dated and labelled "unverified" per this engine's citation standard, and should be treated as directionally reliable but not filing-grade precision — the `moat` agent should re-verify any figure it leans on heavily against the peer's own filing if the comparison is decision-critical.

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — ORCL

## 1. Named Competitors

(Inherited from `08_competitive-map.md` §2 — all three drawn directly from Oracle's own FY26 10-K Risk Factors competitor list.)

- **Microsoft Corporation (NasdaqGS:MSFT)** — competes via Azure (cloud infrastructure, direct OCI rival) and Dynamics 365 (applications, rival to Fusion/NetSuite).
- **Amazon.com, Inc. (NasdaqGS:AMZN)** — competes via AWS, cloud infrastructure only, direct OCI rival.
- **SAP SE (XTRA:SAP)** — competes in cloud/on-premise enterprise applications (ERP), direct rival to Oracle Fusion and NetSuite.

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y (weak-moderate, uneven) | Oracle AI Database is described in its own filing as "the world's most popular enterprise database" [FY26 10-K, Item 1 Business, p.~3763], underpinning a support-renewal annuity that held roughly flat ($19,804M, +1% y/y) even as license revenue fell 9% [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, "Revenues by Offerings," p.45]. But in the fastest-growing segment (OCI), Oracle's own risk factors admit it competes on price against Microsoft, Amazon and Google, not brand pull: "Our competitors may offer lower pricing on their support offerings, which could put pressure on us to further discount" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5994]. | 40 |
| Cost advantage | N | No evidence of a unit-cost advantage that shows up in the numbers. Oracle markets Exadata/OCI as "cost-effective" and performance-optimized relative to competitors [FY26 10-K, Item 1 Business, p.~3548], but this is Oracle's own unverified marketing language, not an independently confirmed cost edge — and the economics run the opposite way: GAAP gross margin has fallen every year for five straight years, from 80.6% (FY21) to 65.8% (FY26) [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab; `07_business-quality.md` §1], the signature of a company spending its way into capacity, not one earning a structural cost edge over AWS (35.4% AWS-segment operating margin, FY2025 [`08_competitive-map.md` §2, Competitor B]) or Azure. | 15 |
| Distribution | Y (real but two-sided) | Oracle's database is sold natively inside its named rivals' own clouds — Database@Azure, Database@AWS and Oracle Multicloud Database services run "within other hyperscale cloud IT environments" [FY26 10-K, Item 1 Business, p.~3622]. This piggybacks Oracle's software distribution on Microsoft's and Amazon's own sales channels, a genuine and unusual distribution advantage. But the filing itself flags the two-edged risk: "This multicloud strategy could lead our customers to migrate away from our cloud offerings to our competitors' products" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5982] — the same channel that extends Oracle's reach also exposes its installed base to competitor upsell. | 45 |
| Scale | N (in the segment that matters most) | Oracle holds roughly 3% of global cloud-infrastructure spend versus AWS 28%, Azure 21% and Google Cloud 14% [`08_competitive-map.md` §3, Web: Synergy Research Group, 2026 (unverified, dated)] — a clear scale disadvantage against the two named infrastructure rivals. In enterprise applications/ERP, Oracle has real installed-base scale (large existing license base), but this is a legacy annuity, not a growth-segment scale edge, and SAP's cloud backlog (+27%) is growing faster than Oracle's cloud applications (+11%) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2–3]. | 25 |
| Technology / IP | Y (real, not decisive) | Oracle discloses "a number of U.S. and foreign patents and pending applications" but states plainly that "neither our business as a whole nor any of our principal businesses are materially dependent on a single patent" [FY26 10-K, Item 1 Business, p.~3986] — i.e., Oracle itself does not claim patent-based defensibility. Database engineering depth (Exadata, Autonomous AI Database) is real technology, but the 10-K's own competitive framing treats the market as fast-moving and low-barrier: "due to the low barriers to entry in many of our market segments, new technologies and new and growing competitors frequently emerge" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~4]. | 35 |
| Licenses / regulation | N (not a differentiator vs these three) | Government-cloud authorizations (FedRAMP, DoW Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification) are real compliance barriers to entry generally [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~7091], but Microsoft (Azure Government) and Amazon (AWS GovCloud) hold equivalent authorizations, so this does not moat Oracle against the three named competitors specifically — it is a cost of doing business in the segment, not a differentiated edge. | 10 |
| Network effects | N | No evidence of classic network effects (value rising with each additional user) in the data pool. Oracle's ecosystem (partners, marketplace) is a distribution channel, not a network-effect moat — not proven from available data. | 5 |
| Switching costs | Y (strongest of the ten) | "Mission-critical databases and ERP systems are costly and risky to replace" underpins the stable support-renewal annuity even as new license sales shrink [`07_business-quality.md` §1]. This shows up directly in the numbers: support revenue held at $19,804M (+1% y/y) despite license revenue falling 9% [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, p.45] — customers keep paying for support on software they are no longer buying more of, the textbook signature of switching-cost lock-in. The filing's own risk factor on errors reinforces this: "Enterprise customers rely on our cloud, software and hardware offerings and related services to run their businesses" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5968]. | 65 |
| Natural resource access | N | Not an advantage — the opposite. Power and GPU access are scarce inputs Oracle must compete for, not resources it controls better than named peers; `10_external-dependency.md` §1 scores commodity/power dependence High risk, and Oracle itself describes power as "constrained globally" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.18, cited in `10_external-dependency.md` §1]. | 5 |
| Location advantage | N | Not proven from available data. No filing evidence that Oracle's data-center site selection confers a location edge over Microsoft, Amazon or SAP specifically; site access is instead flagged as a general execution risk (permitting, power, zoning) [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.~5838, cited in `10_external-dependency.md` §1]. | 10 |

The two moat sources with real evidence are **switching costs** (65/100) in the legacy database/ERP annuity, and, more weakly, **distribution** via multicloud embedding (45/100) and **brand** (40/100) in the support base. The other seven are not proven, or are net negatives (cost advantage, scale, natural-resource access) in the segment now driving results.

## 3. Competitive Economics

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Oracle (ORCL) | 65.8% | 33.2% | 8.22% (CIQ "Return on Capital %," ending-capital basis, reported tax); **~8.5–10.5%** on this agent's own computed basis (see below) | FY26 (FYE May-31-2026) | CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab; FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A p.45 |
| Microsoft (MSFT) | 67.9% | 46.8% | ~21% (TTM, third-party estimate) | LTM as of 2026-08-13 (margins); ~Mar-2026 (ROIC) | Capital IQ Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-08-13 [`08_competitive-map.md` §2]; Web: GuruFocus/valuesense.io ROIC aggregators, 2026-08-14 (unverified, third-party estimate, methodology not disclosed) |
| Amazon (AMZN, consolidated; AWS segment operating margin shown separately) | Consolidated margin not in this pool | AWS segment op. margin 35.4% (FY2025), 39.4% (Q2 2026) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2] | ~11–12% (TTM, consolidated, third-party estimate) | FY2025 / Q2 2026 (margins, web-sourced); ~Mar-2026 (ROIC) | Web: Amazon FY2025/Q2 2026 earnings coverage, 2026 (unverified, dated) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2]; Web: GuruFocus ROIC aggregator, 2026-08-14 (unverified, third-party estimate) |
| SAP SE (SAP) | 73.7% | 28.8% | ~12–14% (TTM/FY2025, third-party estimate; company reports a rising trend, 7.9% FY2023 → 13.6% FY2025) | LTM as of 2026-08-13 (margins); FY2025 (ROIC trend) | Capital IQ Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as of 2026-08-13 [`08_competitive-map.md` §2]; Web: GuruFocus/Alpha Spread ROIC aggregators, 2026-08-14 (unverified, third-party estimate) |

Peer ROIC figures were flagged by `08_competitive-map.md` §5 as "not available in the Capital IQ comp export pulled" — this agent re-sourced them from web aggregators (GuruFocus, Alpha Spread, valuesense.io) since no peer 10-K/annual report sits in `data/ORCL/`. These are **Level 2, third-party, unverified web estimates** (§4/§6), directionally useful but not filing-grade precision, and each source uses its own undisclosed ROIC methodology (visible in the ~1-3pt spread between sources for the same company). They are shown for context only; the decisive test below runs on Oracle's own filing-sourced numbers.

**Oracle's own computed ROIC (this agent's calculation, standard base).** NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − normalized tax rate). EBIT (GAAP operating income) FY26 = $22,385M [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Income Statement tab]. The FY26 **reported** effective tax rate was 12.6% ($2,467M tax / $19,554M EBT incl. unusual items) [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Income Statement & Ratios tabs] — but Oracle's own 10-K discloses this rate is depressed by one-off items: excluding stock-based compensation, intangible amortization, restructuring, a deferred-tax benefit from a prior legal-entity realignment, and the one-time remeasurement impact of the U.S. "One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act," **the company's own disclosed normalized effective tax rate is 19.9% for FY26 (19.7% for FY25), versus the 12.6% (12.1%) reported rate** [FY26 10-K, Note 12 Income Taxes, p.~12558]. This agent uses Oracle's own 19.9% normalized rate, per the same normalization discipline the DCF orb applies to its own NOPAT — **stripped items: stock-based compensation, intangible amortization, restructuring, the FY2021 legal-entity-realignment deferred-tax benefit, and the FY26 One Big Beautiful Bill Act deferred-tax remeasurement.**

- NOPAT (normalized) = $22,385M × (1 − 0.199) = **$17,930M**.
- Invested capital (Total Debt + Total Equity, CIQ basis): FY25 ending $129,921M; FY26 ending $210,488M [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Balance Sheet tab]. Note: CIQ's "Total Debt" ($167,432M FY26) includes finance/operating lease liabilities beyond the $129,541M of "notes payable and other borrowings" disclosed in the 10-K balance sheet itself [FY26 10-K, Note 6, p.~58017] — both bases are shown because they diverge materially and should not be conflated.
- **Ending-capital ROIC (FY26, normalized tax):** $17,930M / $210,488M = **8.52%** — close to, and cross-checking, CIQ's own headline 8.22% (CIQ's figure implicitly uses the lower 12.6% reported tax rate on a similar capital base: $22,385M × 0.874 = $19,565M / $210,488M ≈ 9.30%, still landing in the same 8–9% band; the exact few points of divergence from CIQ's 8.22% likely reflect a different capital-base definition CIQ does not disclose).
- **Average-capital ROIC (FY26, normalized tax, capital base averaged FY25–FY26 to smooth the year's near-doubling of the balance sheet):** $17,930M / [($129,921M+$210,488M)/2] = $17,930M / $170,205M = **10.53%**.

Both computed figures (8.5% ending-capital, 10.5% average-capital) **cross-check against, and materially confirm, the CIQ headline (8.22%)** rather than diverging from it — no red flag of misread.

**The economic moat test (required).**

> Return on capital **at or below** cost of capital: **~8.5–10.5% ROIC** (Oracle, FY26, own-computed, ending-to-average capital range) vs **~11.2% WACC** (CAPM-based estimate: risk-free rate 4.7% [Web: 10-year US Treasury yield, 2026-08-12 (dated, unverified)] + 5-year beta 1.72 [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab; NYSE:ORCL Public Company Profile, "Beta 5Y"] × 5.0% equity-risk-premium estimate → cost of equity ~13.3%; after-tax cost of debt ~4.25% from FY26 senior-note coupons averaging ~5.3% [FY26 10-K, Note 6, p.~22247-22389] × (1−19.9%); market-value weights ~77% equity / ~23% debt using $441,519M market cap [NYSE:ORCL Public Company Profile] and $129,541M notes payable [FY26 10-K, Note 6, p.~58017]) — **Inference, not from filings; no company-disclosed WACC or hurdle rate exists in this data pool.** Gap: roughly **−70 to −270 basis points** below the estimated cost of capital, depending on which capital basis is used.

No company-disclosed cost of capital exists (checked FY26 10-K, transcripts, investor deck — no hurdle rate or WACC stated). The CAPM estimate above is clearly labeled inference. Because the gap is close (a few tens to a couple hundred basis points, well inside the uncertainty band of a CAPM estimate whose beta, ERP and debt-cost inputs are all approximations), the honest read is that Oracle's return on capital sits **at, or modestly below, its estimated cost of capital** — not comfortably above it.

**Through-cycle read.** CIQ's own "Return on Capital %" series has declined every year for four straight years: FY22 12.35% → FY23 10.54% → FY24 10.07% → FY25 9.62% → FY26 8.22% [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab]. The 5-year average is **~10.2%** — itself close to or below the ~11.2% WACC estimate, so this is not a case of a single depressed peak year distorting the read; the trend has been declining for four years running, and FY26 (the year with by far the largest capital deployment — capex 82.6% of revenue [`07_business-quality.md` §1]) is the low point of that trend, not an outlier peak. Per `07_business-quality.md` §4, this decline coincides with, and is caused by, the OCI capital build-out outrunning the earnings it has not yet produced.

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers:** Oracle sits at the **bottom of named peers** on both margin and computed return on capital. LTM EBIT margin (33.2%) trails Microsoft (46.8%) and is roughly in line with SAP (28.8%, Oracle ahead) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2]; on return on capital, Oracle's own-computed ~8.5–10.5% trails Microsoft's third-party-estimated ~21% and SAP's ~12–14%, and is roughly comparable to or below Amazon's consolidated ~11–12% (noting Amazon's AWS-segment margin of 35.4–39.4% is itself well above Oracle's consolidated margin) [§3 above].
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test):** the company earns a return on capital **at or modestly below** its estimated cost of capital (~8.5–10.5% vs ~11.2% WACC, Inference, not from filings) — the decisive test, and it is not comfortably cleared.

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Narrow moat**, capped there by the hard rule in §5 of this report's instructions: Oracle's own-computed and CIQ-cross-checked return on capital (~8.5–10.5%, through-cycle average ~10.2%) sits at or modestly below its estimated ~11.2% cost of capital, so a "Strong moat" verdict is foreclosed regardless of the genuine peer-relative weakness that already argues against it. This is close to the **"moat in structure, not economics"** case: **switching costs** are real and evidenced (support revenue held flat at $19,804M even as license revenue fell 9%, the signature of customers locked into a legacy database/ERP annuity they are not expanding but cannot leave [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, p.45]), but that structural advantage sits inside a consolidated business whose capital-weighted return does not clear its cost of capital, because the dominant, capital-hungry part of the business (OCI) is being built at a pace and cost that has pulled the whole company's return on capital down for four straight years. The durability test over the next five years is whether the ~$638 billion RPO order book converts to recognized, cash-generative revenue fast enough for the return on capital to durably clear its cost of capital — or whether the legacy switching-cost annuity keeps shrinking as a share of the business while the low-return infrastructure buildout keeps growing as a share of it. Because the industry rate-of-change/disruption row in `07_business-quality.md` scored 33 (≤40, Filter 5), this durability test must be discounted further: a moat judgment made mid-AI-infrastructure-cycle is inherently harder to underwrite than the same judgment in a stable, slow-moving industry (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 5).

**Moat trajectory: eroding.** Return on capital vs. cost of capital has moved the wrong way for four consecutive years (CIQ Return on Capital % 12.35% FY22 → 8.22% FY26, a period during which the estimated ~11.2% WACC did not move nearly as much) [CIQ Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab; §3 above]. Market-share evidence points the same direction in the segment that increasingly defines the company: Oracle holds ~3% of cloud infrastructure spend against a "Big Three" holding 63% [`08_competitive-map.md` §3-4], and in applications, SAP's cloud/backlog growth (27%) is outpacing Oracle's cloud-applications growth (11%) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2-3]. Pricing power is explicitly contested by the 10-K's own language on competitor discounting [FY26 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p.~5994]. The one countervailing, evidenced fact — the support-renewal annuity holding flat despite a shrinking license base — is a sign the legacy switching-cost moat itself is stable, not eroding on its own; it is the consolidated economics that are eroding because the legacy annuity is a shrinking share of a business now dominated by a low-return capital build-out. This eroding trajectory is the early-warning signal that should feed the permanent-impairment / declining-perpetuity checks in the valuation module's DCF (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 5).

# External Dependency Check — ORCL

*Note: the Risk Score in Section 4 is INVERTED — higher = worse (more dangerous external dependence).*

## 1. Dependency Table

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices (power / energy, GPU hardware) | High | Oracle's growth story now runs through the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) build-out, and that build-out is gated by two scarce physical inputs it does not control: electric power and NVIDIA GPUs. The company itself says power is "constrained globally," that power prices "can be volatile," and that energy-cost increases "can adversely affect our margins, particularly where customer pricing is fixed or committed." | "We have faced, and may continue to face, challenges with securing reliable and cost-effective power sources for our data center energy demands, which are constrained globally... power prices can be volatile" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.18 (Risk Factors)]; Oracle asked FERC to expedite a natural-gas pipeline order because, without it, "the power plant that will generate electricity for the data center campus cannot function" for the Doña Ana ("Project Jupiter") site [FY26 10-K pool — Key Developments, 2026-05-05 FERC filing]; OCI Zettascale10 cluster is built on "hundreds of thousands of NVIDIA GPUs" [Key Developments, 2025-10-14]; global GPU utilization cited at 97.5%, implying no spare capacity buffer [Q4 FY26 transcript, Jun-10-2026, CEO Magouyrk prepared remarks] |
| Interest rates | High | Outstanding debt was $129.5 billion as of May 31, 2026, almost all raised to fund the AI data-center build-out, and management plans to raise roughly $40 billion more in debt and equity in FY27. A downgrade would raise borrowing costs, could shrink access to commercial paper, and — unusually — could "limit eligibility to contract with certain customers." One Term Loan facility (SOFR-based) was swapped from floating to fixed via cash-flow hedges, but the company continues to issue large volumes of new fixed-rate notes into whatever rate environment prevails at issuance. | "As of May 31, 2026, we had an aggregate of $129.5 billion of outstanding indebtedness" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.19]; "a downgrade could also reduce our access to, or increase the cost of, commercial paper... limit eligibility to contract with certain customers" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.19]; "we expect to raise around $40 billion in debt and equity in our fiscal year '27" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CFO Maxson]; FY26 senior-note issuance of $43.0 billion par value across 13 tranches, most fixed-rate, one $500 million floating-rate tranche due Feb-2029 [FY26 10-K, Note 12/13 (Debt)] |
| FX | Mid | A large share of revenue and expense is booked outside the U.S. and translated into U.S. Dollars. The company quantifies the exposure and partially hedges it with rolling forward contracts, so the dependency is real but managed, not a pass-through. | "10% decrease in foreign currency exchange rates" → Earnings impact of $(2,767) million in fiscal 2026 vs. $(2,379) million in fiscal 2025 [FY26 10-K, Item 7A, Sensitivity Analysis table, p.56] — roughly 4% of FY26 total revenue of ~$67 billion [Q4 FY26 transcript, CFO Maxson: "we surpassed revenues of $67 billion for the first time"]; "we have a program which primarily utilizes foreign currency forward contracts... may suspend the program from time to time... may not fully offset" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.19] |
| Government policy | High | Government is both a direct customer (VA, Office of Personnel Management) and a gatekeeper for the physical infrastructure Oracle needs. The Doña Ana, New Mexico "Project Jupiter" Stargate site cannot function without a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order approving a gas pipeline, and Oracle's own regulatory filing ties the project explicitly to "the President's priority goal" on AI infrastructure — i.e., the pace of a multi-billion-dollar build is sitting inside a federal approval queue. | "Our sales to local, state, federal and foreign government customers expose us to business volatility and risks, including government budgeting cycles and appropriations, government shutdowns... governmental policy shifts" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.16]; "the United States Government Office of Personnel Management today announced an agency-wide award to Oracle for Fusion HCM" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Sicilia]; "delay would directly undermine the national security and economic imperatives identified by the President" — Oracle's own FERC filing on the Green Chile pipeline needed to power Project Jupiter [Key Developments, 2026-05-05] |
| Regulation | Mid | Export-control/sanctions rules can block Oracle from serving certain customers with GPU-enabled cloud capacity; data-center siting is subject to zoning, environmental, water-use and data-localization rules; Oracle Health is separately subject to healthcare regulation. These are real constraints on where and how OCI can be built and sold, but they are diversified across many jurisdictions rather than concentrated in one regulator's hands. | "Evolving restrictions and rules governing access to cloud-based infrastructure or GPU-enabled services by customers in certain jurisdictions... could prevent us from serving certain customers" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.13]; "Government-imposed limits or moratoria on data center construction in a given market could hinder our ability to execute our expansion plans" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.18]; "The healthcare industry is highly regulated... non-compliance... could adversely affect our healthcare business" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, Risk Factor Summary, p.16] |
| Weather | Low | Weather shows up only as a secondary driver of power-price volatility and as one item in a general business-continuity list (storms, drought, pandemics); it is not a line item management quantifies or treats as a primary swing factor. | "power prices can be volatile, including due to extreme weather events" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.18]; "the effects of climate change (such as increased storm severity, drought and pandemics)" listed among disaster-recovery risks to critical operations [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.20] |
| Geopolitics | Mid | International operations are "concentrated in a few geographic areas, some of which include emerging market international locations that may be less stable," and U.S. sanctions/export-control policy can directly cut off customers from OCI's GPU-based services. Trade-policy and tariff language recurs across all three of Oracle's businesses (cloud/software, hardware, services) as a demand driver. | "A significant portion of our critical business operations are concentrated in a few geographic areas, some of which include emerging market international locations that may be less stable" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.20]; "the effects of inflation, tariffs and trade policy, geopolitical conditions and other macroeconomic factors on customer demand" cited for cloud/software, hardware and services revenue drivers alike [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, p.32–33] |
| Industrial cycle (enterprise IT / AI capex cycle) | High | Oracle's near-term growth is now a bet on a small number of very large AI infrastructure buyers continuing to commit capital. Remaining performance obligations (contracted, unrecognized revenue) jumped from $138 billion to $638 billion in a single year — a 363% increase — driven by "certain significant cloud contracts," and management itself named the concentration: "4 customers contracting for more than $8 billion this quarter." A February 2026 company statement named the customers underpinning the capital raise directly: "AMD, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, TikTok, xAI and others." If the AI infrastructure investment cycle among a handful of hyperscale/AI-lab buyers slows or any one of these counterparties pulls back, the built-but-uncontracted capacity (or capacity built on leases that outlast customer contract terms) becomes a stranded cost, not a revenue stream. | "Remaining performance obligations were $638 billion and $138 billion as of May 31, 2026 and 2025, respectively... primarily attributable to certain significant cloud contracts" [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A, p.55]; "our remaining performance obligations, or RPO, finished at $638 billion, up 363%" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CFO Maxson]; "we continue to diversify across our largest customers with 4 customers contracting for more than $8 billion this quarter" [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Magouyrk]; "In certain OCI offerings, we are more concentrated among a number of large customers, which could increase these risks [of customer non-payment/non-performance]" [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.18]; "Oracle is raising money in order to build additional capacity to meet the contracted demand from our largest Oracle Cloud Infrastructure customers, including AMD, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, TikTok, xAI and others" [Key Developments, 2026-02-02, company statement]; a securities class action was filed alleging Oracle overstated the AI-deal growth outlook, with the stock falling 5.6% on a September 2025 analyst downgrade of AI-revenue credibility and 10.8% on a December 2025 capex-guidance miss [Key Developments, 2026-02-05] |

*Rows dropped as not materially applicable: Freight/logistics rates (Oracle is a software/cloud/hardware company; equipment-delivery timing is an execution risk inside "data center capacity," not a freight-cost dependency the filings quantify separately). Consumer cycle (Oracle sells to enterprises, governments and institutions, not consumers directly; the relevant demand-cycle exposure is captured under Industrial cycle above).*

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Variable | Hypothetical Move | Disclosed Impact (FY2026) | Disclosed Impact (FY2025) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FX — total revenues/earnings | 10% decrease in foreign currency exchange rates | $(2,767) million | $(2,379) million | FY26 10-K, Item 7A, Sensitivity Analysis table, p.56 |
| FX — cash, cash equivalents and trade receivables, net (fair value) | 10% decrease in foreign currency exchange rates | $(2,384) million | $(1,788) million | FY26 10-K, Item 7A, Sensitivity Analysis table, p.56 |

Oracle does not publish a quantified interest-rate sensitivity table in Item 7A (Item 7A covers only currency risk in this filing) despite $129.5 billion of debt outstanding — a gap in disclosure given the scale of the balance sheet [FY26 10-K, Item 7A, p.55–56, reviewed in full: only "Currency Risk" subsections present]. This is Not proven from available data as a quantified figure; the qualitative risk-factor language on rate/refinancing risk is cited in Section 1 above.

## 3. Classification

**Mostly externally driven.**

Two years ago this would have read "Partly externally driven" — a large, diversified enterprise software company with real pricing power and only moderate FX and government-budget exposure. That is no longer the shape of the business the market is pricing. FY26 remaining performance obligations exploded 363% to $638 billion on the back of a handful of AI-infrastructure customers (four contracts over $8 billion each in a single quarter, contracted counterparties publicly named as AMD, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, TikTok and xAI). Funding that backlog into delivered capacity requires Oracle to keep winning a scarce, contested physical input (data-center power) and a scarce, single-sourced-by-vendor physical input (NVIDIA GPUs), while raising roughly $40 billion a year in fresh debt and equity — on top of $129.5 billion of debt already outstanding — into whatever capital-markets conditions and credit-rating outcome prevail at the time. Management retains real levers (which sites to build, which customers to prioritize, hedging of FX and some interest-rate exposure, pricing of new contracts), which is why this is not scored as a pure pass-through — but the dominant swing factors in next twelve to thirty-six months of results (whether RPO actually converts to revenue, whether power and GPU supply keep pace, whether debt gets raised on acceptable terms) sit substantially outside management's control.

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**72/100** (higher = worse; inverted scale — see note at top of report)

Drivers of the score: customer/counterparty concentration inside the AI infrastructure backlog (High), physical-input scarcity in power and GPUs gating whether that backlog can be delivered (High), and a debt load that has nearly doubled in a year with no slowdown in appetite for more (High) together outweigh the genuinely well-managed and disclosed FX hedging program (Mid) and the historically diversified, if policy-exposed, government and regulatory book (Government policy High, Regulation Mid). This sits in the 61–80 "mostly externally driven, limited management levers" band rather than the 81–100 "pure pass-through" band because Oracle still chooses which data-center sites to build, which customers to prioritize capacity for, and retains a large legacy database/applications franchise (cloud and software was 87% of FY26 revenue) that is not directly hostage to the AI capex cycle in the same way OCI is.

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

If AI-infrastructure demand from Oracle's largest named OCI customers (AMD, Meta, NVIDIA, OpenAI, TikTok, xAI) pulled back 20% from what is embedded in the $638 billion remaining-performance-obligation backlog, the damage would exceed any single FX, rate or power-cost move: Oracle would be left holding data-center leases, power-purchase commitments and ~$129.5 billion of debt sized to a demand level that no longer exists, with margins already compressed from the current build-out ramp — the classic "locked into multi-year commitments for excess data center space and related capital expenditures... without receiving corresponding revenue" scenario the company itself flags [FY26 10-K, Item 1A, p.18].

# Capital Allocation & Governance — ORCL

## 1. Signal Table

Severity is INVERTED — higher score = worse.

## 2. Classification

**Capital allocation concerns.**

The table is not dominated by governance red flags in the classic sense — there is no fraud signal, no auditor qualification, no restatement, and the controlling insider's stake has been stable for years. The concern is capital allocation: capex has been allowed to outrun operating cash flow so completely that FY26 levered free cash flow (cash from operations of $32.0bn minus total capex of $55.7bn) was -$24.5bn [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab], the dividend ($5.8bn paid FY26) is now funded from debt and preferred-stock proceeds rather than from free cash flow, total debt rose 54% in a single year to $167.4bn, and S&P responded with a downgrade to BBB- on Jul-09-2026 [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Key Developments.xls]. Buybacks have effectively stopped and the historical multi-year share-count reduction has reversed into renewed dilution. None of this is a proven value-destruction event yet — management frames it as demand-backed growth investment tied to a $638bn remaining-performance-obligation (RPO) book [Q4 FY26 earnings call, Jun-10-2026] — but the scale and speed of the debt-funded buildout, on top of the CEO and CFO both changing within the same fiscal year, is a material capital-allocation and balance-sheet risk that this agent flags for the synthesis and for the balance-sheet-survival module.

## 3. Most Material Signal

The debt-level-and-trajectory row is the one that would most change this classification if it worsens further. Total debt already rose 54% in a single fiscal year, net debt/(EBITDA-capex) is no longer a computable ratio because capex now exceeds all of EBITDA, and S&P has already cut the rating to BBB- — one downgrade notch from losing investment-grade status. Management has guided FY27 net capex to roughly $70bn, higher again than FY26's $48bn net outlay [Q4 FY26 earnings call, Jun-10-2026], which means the debt trajectory is not a one-off — it is scheduled to continue. If a further downgrade below investment grade occurs, or if the AI-cloud demand behind the $638bn RPO does not convert into cash on the schedule management expects, this moves from "capital allocation concerns" to a balance-sheet-survival question, which is the sharper test this agent's evidence points toward but does not itself adjudicate.

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**42/100.**

No rejector-filter cap applies: the acquisition-pattern row scored 30/100, well below the 70 severity threshold for the Filter 4 serial-acquirer cap (CLAUDE.md §24, MODULE_RULES.md), since Oracle's M&A has been two large, spaced-out deals over a decade with no goodwill impairment recorded — not a pattern of continuous, debt-funded serial acquisitions.

The 42/100 reflects clean mechanical governance (auditor tenure, no restatements, no related-party entanglement, stable controlling insider) weighed against a genuinely weak capital-discipline picture: negative free cash flow, a debt-funded dividend, a 54%-in-one-year debt increase, a credit downgrade already realized, and a CEO/CFO transition landing in the same year as the largest leverage increase in the company's history. This score should be read together with the balance-sheet-survival module's leverage and refinancing-risk findings, which this agent's debt-trajectory evidence directly feeds.

# Red Flags Sweep — ORCL

## 1. Already Covered Upstream

| Upstream Agent | Flag Already Surfaced |
