**Founder/owner-operator status:** Oracle is founder-influenced but not founder-run. Larry Ellison founded the company and remains Executive Chair, CTO and its largest shareholder at ~40.2% of common stock [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Public Ownership Summary.rtf, Top Holders table, "Ellison, Lawrence J., 1,158,232,353 shares, 40.21%"], but he stepped down as CEO in 2014 and the operating CEO role now sits with two non-founder, internal-promotion co-CEOs. This is a hybrid: a founder-controlled board with professional-manager day-to-day leadership, not a classic owner-operator CEO structure.

## 2. Management Stability

| Signal | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Senior departures (last 3 years) | CEO Safra Catz stepped down after 11 years (Sept 2025) into a Board role (not an exit from the company); no CFO, General Counsel, or Chief Accounting Officer departure in the period beyond the CFO seat transition below. Two long-tenured independent directors (George Conrades, 18 years; Naomi Seligman, 20 years) retired in Jan 2026, replaced by two new independent directors (Rusckowski, Nov 2025; Mihaljevic, May 2026) — framed as ordinary board refreshment, not resignations citing concerns | [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Key Developments.xls, "Executive and Board Changes, Effective September 22, 2025"; "Retirement of Directors George H. Conrades and Naomi O. Seligman," 2026-01-09; "Names Stephen Rusckowski to the Board," 2025-11-21; "Elects Dr. Tomislav Mihaljevic to Board," 2026-05-12] |
| CFO turnover | **Two CFO-seat changes inside an 8-month window**: Catz (CFO through 2014, by then long removed from the role) → interim Principal Financial Officer Doug Kehring (Sept 22, 2025) → external hire Hilary Maxson (Apr 6, 2026). This lands in the same fiscal year Oracle raised total debt 54% (to $167.4bn) and was downgraded by S&P to BBB- (Jul 9, 2026) [`business-model/11_capital-allocation-governance.md`] — a CFO seat in flux during the company's largest-ever leverage and capex ramp is a genuine stability warning, even though each individual step (internal bridge, then an experienced external hire) was orderly rather than a sudden resignation | [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Key Developments.xls, CFO-change entries above] |
| CEO succession / continuity | Oracle moved from a single, 11-year CEO (Catz) to an **unprecedented co-CEO structure** (Magouyrk/Sicilia) — both internal promotions with 11+ and 16+ years at the company respectively, not outside hires, which reduces (but does not eliminate) execution risk from the transition. The 10-K states there were "no arrangements or understandings between Mr. Magouyrk and any other persons pursuant to which he was appointed" — standard SEC succession language, not independently verified evidence of a smooth transition | [FY26 10-K, Item 10]; [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Key Developments.xls, 2025-09-22 entries] |

**Read:** the CEO transition itself is lower-risk than it looks — both new co-CEOs are long-tenured internal operators, and the bridge CFO (Kehring, 26 years at Oracle) prevented a leadership vacuum. The CFO seat is the more genuine warning: two changes in 8 months, with the incoming CFO having zero Oracle-specific track record as of this filing, landing exactly when the balance sheet risk is highest (debt +54% in one year, credit downgrade already realized). This is flagged, not glossed over.

## 3. Stated Strategy & Targets

Management says Oracle is pivoting from an enterprise-software/database incumbent into a large-scale AI cloud-infrastructure (OCI) supplier, funded by a $638 billion remaining performance obligation (RPO) backlog that grew 363% in one year [FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A; Q4 FY26 earnings call, CFO Maxson]. The explicit, checkable targets set on the Jun 10, 2026 (Q4 FY26) call and press release are: FY2027 total revenue of $90 billion (point guidance), FY2027 non-GAAP EPS of $8.05 (raised from a prior figure, ~18% growth once one-time gains are excluded from the base), FY2027 net cash capex of roughly $70 billion (implying gross capex in the $90–95 billion area once customer prepayments are added back), and a capital-financing plan to raise about $40 billion through debt and equity (including the already-announced $20 billion at-the-market equity program), with no additional debt issuance planned in calendar 2026 [Oracle_Earnings Press Release Q4FY26.pdf, "Guidance for Full FY 2027"; Q4 FY26 earnings call, CFO prepared remarks].

## 4. Promise vs Delivery

| Prior Promise / Target | Period Set | Actual Outcome | Kept / Missed | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 capital expenditure level implied by guidance issued after Q1 FY26 (~Sept 2025) | Set ~Sept 2025 (post-Q1 FY26 call) | On the Dec 10, 2025 (Q2 FY26) call, Oracle disclosed it "now expect[ed] fiscal 2026 CapEx will be about $15 billion higher than [it] forecasted after Q1," alongside a revenue-growth and free-cash-flow miss versus Street consensus that quarter. Stock fell $24.16 (−10.8%) the next day | **Missed** — capex ran materially above what was signaled just one quarter earlier | [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Key Developments.xls, 2026-02-05 entry quoting the Q2 FY26 print and stock reaction] |
| FQ1 FY2026 revenue and EPS (Street-consensus-referenced, no separate Oracle point guidance found for the specific quarter in the pool) | Guided ~Jun 2025 | Actual revenue $14,926M vs estimate $15,043M (−0.78%); actual non-GAAP EPS $1.47 vs estimate $1.479 (−0.68%) | **Missed** (narrowly, on both lines) | [`earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md`, Section 6, citing Capital IQ Estimates Report Surprise tab] |
| FQ2 FY2026 revenue and EPS | Guided ~Sept 2025 | Revenue missed by −0.83%; non-GAAP EPS beat by +37.8%, but the beat was driven by one-time investment gains (Ampere/Bloom Energy), not operating performance — GAAP EPS beat by +79.5% the same quarter | **Mixed / not a clean operating beat** — the headline EPS "beat" overstates underlying delivery | [`earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md`, Section 6] |
| FQ3 FY2026 revenue and EPS | Guided ~Dec 2025 | Revenue beat +1.66%; EPS beat +5.9%, no footnoted one-off | **Kept / clean beat** | [`earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md`, Section 6] |
| FQ4 FY2026 revenue and EPS | Guided ~Mar 2026 | Revenue beat +0.46%; EPS beat +7.65% headline, but $2.7bn Ampere-sale gain and Bloom Energy warrant gains inflated the figure — ex-gains non-GAAP EPS was $2.03 (vs. $1.962 estimate), a genuine but smaller beat of +3.4% | **Kept, but smaller than headline once one-offs are stripped** | [`earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md`, Section 6; FY26 10-K, Item 7 MD&A "Non-Operating Income (Expense), Net"] |
| FY2027 revenue $90bn / non-GAAP EPS $8.05 (current guidance) | Set Jun 10, 2026 | Not yet reportable — first FY2027 print is FQ1 FY2027, due Sept 4, 2026, after this run's date | **Not yet assessable** — flagged for the next earnings cycle | [`earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md`, Section 2–3] |

**Net read:** across the four most recent reported quarters, Oracle beat on revenue in 2 of 4 and beat on EPS in 3 of 4 as reported, but once the one-time Ampere/Bloom Energy gains are stripped from two of those EPS "beats," the clean operating beat rate falls to roughly 2 of 4 — closer to a coin flip than a track record of reliably beating its own numbers [`earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md`, Section 6]. The one specific, dated promise that clearly broke was the FY2026 capex level: management under-forecast its own capital spending by about $15 billion within a single quarter, and the market punished it (−10.8% same-week reaction). Set against that, current FY2027 guidance sits within roughly ±0.1%–0.7% of Street consensus on revenue and EPS [`earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md`, Section 3] — management is not currently sandbagging or over-promising versus what analysts already expect, which is a different (and better) signal than the FY2026 capex miss, but it also means the FY2027 numbers have not yet been tested against actual delivery.

(not evidence) | Partially relevant even without a turnaround framing: the new co-CEOs' and CFO's résumés (AWS engineering background, Schneider Electric capital-intensive-infrastructure CFO experience) are being implicitly cited by the company and by sell-side commentary as reasons the leadership team can execute the AI-infrastructure build-out. This report treats those résumés as background, not as evidence of delivery — the delivery test is the promise-vs-delivery table in Section 4, not the biographies in Section 1 | [FY26 10-K, Item 10] |

**Turnaround rule application:** Not applicable — see row 1. Oracle is classified as an established, growing incumbent undergoing a capital-intensive strategic pivot with new leadership, not a governance-turnaround thesis.

**Integrity rule application:** This report chased the routed signal as far as the data pool allows. The pool contains: the plaintiffs' factual narrative (a law-firm press release, not a court filing or company admission), the underlying disclosed facts it is built on (the capex-guidance revision, the analyst note, the Bloomberg report — all independently corroborated in Key Developments and the 10-K), and the company's own framing (RPO growth, customer-concentration disclosure, and its explicit backing-out of one-time gains from FY2027 guidance). None of the pool's sources — not the 10-K, not the two earnings-call transcripts, not the Key Developments log — contains a motion-to-dismiss ruling, a settlement, an SEC finding, or a company admission that would clear or escalate this allegation. **The signal remains unresolved**, neither cleared by primary evidence nor escalated to a proven fact. Per the module rule, this is emitted as a standalone red flag below.

**RF-MGT-005 (unresolved adverse integrity signal, unproven)** — Securities class action alleging Oracle overstated its AI-infrastructure deal growth outlook (filed Feb 3, 2026, U.S. District Court, District of Delaware; pre-motion-to-dismiss as of the FY26 10-K date). Not cleared by primary evidence; not proven. Caps Management Quality at 60 and conviction at no better than "Watchlist" until resolved, per MODULE_RULES.md Score Cap Rules.

## 5. Management Read

Oracle's leadership bench is deep and internally seasoned — both new co-CEOs are long-tenured Oracle veterans (11 and 16+ years) rather than outside hires, and the 26-year-veteran who bridged the CFO seat prevented a leadership vacuum during the transition — but the CFO chair itself changed hands twice in eight months, landing in the exact fiscal year Oracle's debt rose 54% to $167.4bn and its credit rating was cut to BBB-, which is a genuine timing-and-stability concern, not a cosmetic one. The promise-vs-delivery record is mixed, not clean: the clear, dated miss is the ~$15 billion FY2026 capex-guidance overshoot that management itself disclosed and that cost the stock 10.8% in a day, while the quarterly beat streak that looks strong on the surface (beats in 3 of the last 4 EPS prints) shrinks to roughly a coin flip once one-time Ampere/Bloom Energy gains are stripped out of two of those beats. The single biggest management signal is the unresolved securities class action alleging the AI-deal growth outlook itself was overstated — an allegation this report could not clear or dismiss from the available filings, so it is carried forward as a live, capped risk (RF-MGT-005) rather than discounted because the company's audited financials are otherwise clean.

## management-governance / 02_capital-allocation-scorecard.md

# Capital-Allocation Scorecard — ORCL

Reporting currency: USD. Fiscal year ends May 31 (Oracle "FY2026" = year ended May-31-2026). All figures from audited filings or Capital IQ exports as cited; a discrepancy between Capital IQ's cash-flow-statement buyback figures and the 10-K's own disclosed buyback figures for FY2025/FY2026 is flagged and resolved in favor of the filing per CLAUDE.md §5.

## 1. Uses of Capital (5 years, FY2022–FY2026)

| Use | Cumulative Amount | Currency | % of CFO | Source |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Acquisitions (net cash) | 27,869 | USD mm | 28.4% | [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, "Cash Acquisitions" row, FY2022–FY2026] |
| Buybacks | 23,779 | USD mm | 24.2% | FY2022–FY2024 from [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, "Repurchase of Common Stock"]; FY2025–FY2026 from [FY26 10-K, "Common Stock Repurchase Program," "We repurchased 0.4 million shares for $93 million and 3.9 million shares for $600 million in fiscal 2026 and 2025, respectively"] — the filing's own figures are used for FY25–FY26 in preference to Capital IQ's cash-flow-tab figures of $1,500mm (FY25) and $206mm (FY26), which appear to include a broader repurchase definition (e.g., shares withheld for employee tax on RSU vesting) than the Board-authorized buyback program the 10-K reports on |
| Dividends (common + preferred) | 22,046 | USD mm | 22.5% | [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, "Total Dividends Paid," FY2022–FY2026]; [FY26 10-K, "In fiscal 2026, we declared and paid aggregate cash dividends of $1,263.89 per share of outstanding Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock that totaled $63 million and $2.00 per share of outstanding common stock that totaled $5.7 billion"] |
| Capex | 96,950 | USD mm | 98.8% | [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, "Capital Expenditure," FY2022–FY2026] |
| Debt repayment (scheduled + commercial paper) | 58,035 | USD mm | 59.1% | [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, "Total Debt Repaid," FY2022–FY2026] |
| **Memo: cumulative CFO, FY2022–FY2026** | 98,175 | USD mm | 100% | [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, "Cash from Ops." row] |
| **Memo: cumulative debt + preferred + common-stock issuance, FY2022–FY2026** | 115,763 | USD mm | 117.9% of CFO | [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, "Total Debt Issued" ($106,291mm) + "Issuance of Pref. Stock" ($4,954mm) + "Issuance of Common Stock" ($4,518mm)] |

Total uses of capital over the period ($228,679mm) exceed cumulative cash from operations ($98,175mm) by roughly $130,504mm. That gap was not closed by cutting capex or buybacks — it was closed by raising $115,763mm of new debt, preferred stock and common-stock-plan proceeds over the same five years, concentrated almost entirely in FY2025–FY2026. This is the single structural fact behind every row below: Oracle is now funding its dividend, and a large share of its capex, with borrowed and freshly-raised capital, not with cash the business is throwing off.

## 2. M&A Scorecard

| Deal | Year | Price | Disclosed Rationale / Synergy | Delivered? | Opportunity Cost (divestitures forced / focus lost / options foregone) | Source |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| NetSuite, Inc. | Closed Nov-2016 (FY2017) | $9.3bn cash (Oracle's FY2017 total cash acquisitions of $11,221mm include this deal plus smaller add-ons) | Add a cloud ERP suite for small/mid-market customers Oracle's own on-premise stack did not serve | Not separately assessable — Oracle discloses no standalone NetSuite revenue or return figure; NetSuite is folded into the "Cloud and Software" segment's SaaS applications line with no sub-line breakout in the audited segment note [FY26 10-K, Note 13]. No goodwill impairment has ever been recorded against this deal | Low — the deal was cash-funded at a point when Oracle's capex was modest (~$2.0bn FY2017) and did not force any disclosed divestiture or strategic pivot; limited opportunity cost | [FY26 10-K, Note 13 (Segment Information)]; [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, FY2017 "Cash Acquisitions" row] |
| Cerner Corporation (now "Oracle Health") | Closed Jun-2022 (FY2023) | $28.3bn total deal value; $27,721mm cash paid per the cash-flow statement | Enter healthcare IT / electronic health records, and cross-sell Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) into hospital systems | Not separately assessable — Oracle Health is likewise folded into "Cloud and Software" with no standalone revenue, margin, or synergy-realization disclosure in any filing in the pool. Product-level news (AI patient portal, AI clinical-note agent, Theator surgical-AI partnership) shows continued product investment, not a disclosed financial return. No goodwill impairment has been recorded ("Our most recent goodwill impairment analysis was performed on March 1, 2026 and did not result in a goodwill impairment charge") | Real — the deal was debt-funded: total debt rose from $75,859mm (FY2022) to $90,481mm (FY2023), a $14.6bn increase in the deal year [Financials_Annual.xls, Capital-Structure-Summary tab]. That debt capacity was drawn down three years before Oracle needed to raise $167.4bn of total debt (FY2026) to fund the AI-infrastructure buildout — the Cerner deal consumed leverage headroom that, with hindsight, would have been more valuable held in reserve for the OCI capex cycle that followed. This is the opportunity-cost charge against the deal, separate from and in addition to its own unproven return | [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, FY2023 "Cash Acquisitions" row; Capital-Structure-Summary tab, "Total Debt" row]; [FY26 10-K, Note (Goodwill), "Our most recent goodwill impairment analysis..."]; [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Key-Developments.xls, Cerner/Oracle Health product-announcement entries, 2026] |

**Serial-acquirer test (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 4):** Not triggered. Oracle made two material acquisitions in a ten-year window (NetSuite FY2017, Cerner FY2023), spaced roughly six years apart, with zero cash acquisitions recorded in FY2024, FY2025 or FY2026 [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab]. This is periodic, large-deal M&A, not a continuous serial-acquirer pattern; RF-CAP-004 does not apply, consistent with `business-model/11_capital-allocation-governance.md`'s own conclusion. That said, neither deal carries a disclosed, checkable return metric — "no goodwill impairment" is a floor (the deal has not obviously failed), not evidence the deal cleared its cost of capital. Absent a disclosed synergy target vs. actual, both deals are scored on the opportunity-cost test only, and Cerner fails that test materially given the debt-capacity consumption described above.

There was no stock repurchase activity for the three months ended May 31, 2026"] |

This module runs before the valuation module in the pipeline, so buyback price discipline is judged only against the stock's own trading range within each fiscal year — not against an intrinsic/fair-value estimate. Intrinsic-value discipline is not assessable from this module; if the valuation module's fair-value range becomes available, the FY2025–FY2026 implied prices ($153.85 and $232.50) should be re-tested against it.

**Net read:** buybacks did the heavy lifting on per-share value from FY2017 through the FY2023 trough — diluted shares fell from 4,217mm (FY2017) to 2,766mm (FY2023), a 34.4% reduction [Financials_Annual.xls, Income Statement tab] — but that program has been effectively switched off since FY2024. Diluted share count has now risen for three straight years (2,766mm → 2,914mm, +5.3% off the FY2023 low), buybacks have fallen 99.5% from the FY2022 peak in dollar terms, and stock-based compensation ($4,811mm FY2026) plus a new $5.0bn Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock (convertible into common by Jan-15-2029) point to further dilution ahead with no offsetting repurchase activity. **RF-CAP-002 (buybacks not reducing share count) is triggered for FY2024–FY2026.**

This affects only the FY2021 base-year figure, not the FY2023–FY2026 leg of the computation |

The dividend itself is not large relative to earnings (33.4% payout, and falling) — the problem is not the dividend's size, it is that operations no longer generate enough cash to pay it. Both FY2025 and FY2026 dividends were effectively funded from the $115.8bn of debt, preferred stock, and common-stock-plan proceeds raised over the period (Section 1), not from free cash flow. **RF-CAP-003 (dividends not covered by FCF) is triggered for FY2025–FY2026**, consistent with the flag already raised in `business-model/11_capital-allocation-governance.md` and `01_management-and-track-record.md` (finding 01-013).

Incremental ROIC of 5.3%–7.0% describes the return the last several years of net new capital have earned so far. That return is being generated while the newest and largest tranche of capital — the FY2026 capex ramp ($55.7bn, more than 2.6x FY2025's level) — has barely begun to be reflected in revenue (RPO of $638bn is contracted-but-not-yet-recognized backlog, not realized revenue). This module does not compute or compare against a cost-of-capital figure (that is the valuation module's job), but flags that the incremental-ROIC figure so far is thin relative to the scale of capital being deployed, and its trajectory over the next 2–3 reporting periods is the single most important number for testing whether this capital allocation cycle creates or destroys per-share value.

## 5. Capital-Allocation Read

Capital allocation at Oracle has been mixed, tilting value-destructive on a per-share basis over the most recent two years, after a genuinely value-creative stretch from FY2017–FY2023. The best use of capital in the period was the historical buyback program, which cut diluted shares by 34.4% from FY2017 to the FY2023 trough — real, verifiable per-share value creation — but that program is now effectively dead (FY2026 spend of $93mm is 0.5% of the FY2022 peak), and diluted share count has risen every year since, undoing part of that gain while stock-based compensation and a convertible-preferred overhang keep adding new shares. The worst use of capital is the dividend, not because of its size but because of what funds it: Oracle paid $5.8bn of dividends in FY2026 while free cash flow was −$23.7bn, meaning the payout — and a meaningful share of the AI-infrastructure capex build — is now financed by the $115.8bn of debt, preferred stock and equity-plan proceeds raised over the period, not by the business's own cash generation. The single biggest capital-allocation signal is the sequencing: the debt-funded Cerner acquisition (FY2023) consumed leverage capacity three years before management needed that same capacity for a far larger, AI-driven capex cycle, forcing FY2026's 54% one-year debt increase and the subsequent S&P downgrade to BBB-. Read together with a computed incremental ROIC of only 5.3%–7.0% on the last several years' net new capital, this is not evidence of disciplined per-share compounding — it is a business betting its capital structure on demand (the $638bn RPO backlog) converting to cash on a schedule that has not yet been tested. Verdict: **mixed**, leaning value-destructive on the most recent two years' allocation choices, against a genuinely value-creative earlier record.

# Incentives & Compensation — ORCL

## 1. Compensation Structure

Reporting currency: USD. Period covered: fiscal year 2026 (ended May 31, 2026) and the go-forward target-pay level set in the CFO's January 19, 2026 offer letter. **No 2026 Proxy Statement (DEF 14A) exists yet** — Oracle's FY26 10-K states Items 10–14 (director/executive compensation, ownership, related-party) are "incorporated by reference" from the 2026 Proxy Statement, due within 120 days of the May 31, 2026 fiscal year-end (~Sept 28, 2026) — after this run's date [FY26 10-K, p.59 (Item 11 index) and Items 10–14 cross-reference]. That means there is no Summary Compensation Table, no Compensation Discussion & Analysis, and no disclosed bonus/LTIP metric weights for either co-CEO in the data pool. The one hard, filed exception is an employment offer letter for the new CFO, filed as **Exhibit 10.15** to the FY26 10-K.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|

| Co-CEO Michael D. Sicilia (since Sept 22, 2025) | Insufficient Data | Insufficient Data | Insufficient Data | Insufficient Data | Not disclosed — internal promotion, no offer letter filed; 2026 Proxy not yet filed [FY26 10-K, Item 10] |
| CFO Hilary Maxson (offer accepted Jan 2026, started Apr 6, 2026) | $950,000/yr | Target $2,500,000 at 100% target achievement under the "FY26 Executive Bonus Plan"; overall bonus capped at $5,000,000 (2x target); prorated for FY26 based on start date | Total target grant value $26,000,000: 80% ($20,800,000) time-based equity (employee's choice of 100% stock options, or 50% options / 50% RSUs, vesting 40%/30%/20%/10% over years 1–4) + 20% ($5,200,000) performance-based stock options (PSOs) vesting over a 3-year performance period ending May 31, 2028, "subject to the achievement of certain revenue metrics" | ~3% cash (base) / ~97% cash-plus-target-bonus-and-equity is equity-dominated: base $950K + target bonus $2.5M = $3.45M cash vs $26M target equity, i.e. roughly 88% of total target pay ($29.45M) is equity | [FY26 10-K, Exhibit 10.15 — Offer letter and employment agreement with Hilary Maxson, dated Jan 25, 2026 (offer letter itself dated Jan 19, 2026)] |

Catz (CEO through Sept 22, 2025; Exec Vice Chair since) | Insufficient Data | Insufficient Data | Insufficient Data | Insufficient Data | FY2026 (partial-year, pre-transition) pay not disclosed in the pool; her FY2025 pay lived in the FY2025 Proxy Statement, which is outside this run's data pool and outside the partial-data rule's scope for this report | Not in pool |

**The one concrete, filed data point:** the CFO's performance-based equity — 20% of her total target grant, or $5.2M in target value — is explicitly tied to **"revenue metrics,"** not a per-share or returns metric [Exhibit 10.15]. Note 11 (Stock-Based Compensation Plans) of the FY26 10-K separately confirms company-wide PSOs "vest over tranches probable of achievement" based on "performance-metric achievement," without naming the metric for the broader program [FY26 10-K, Note 11]. Nothing in the pool discloses the CEOs' pay structure at all, and nothing discloses the specific metrics or weights inside the FY26 Executive Bonus Plan itself (only its dollar target and cap for one executive).

No per-share or returns-based metric appears anywhere in the disclosed record.

## 4. Incentive Alignment Read

Oracle's own pay disclosure for this fiscal year is almost entirely absent — the 2026 Proxy Statement that would show both co-CEOs' bonus and LTIP metrics, weights, and dollar totals has not been filed, so alignment cannot be judged at the CEO level at all. The one hard number the pool does give — the new CFO's performance-based stock options, 20% of a $26 million target equity grant, vesting on "certain revenue metrics" rather than any per-share, margin, cash-flow, or returns test — is a size-based metric, and it sits inside a year in which Oracle's levered free cash flow turned sharply negative (−$24.5bn) and total debt rose 54% while capex ran roughly $15bn ahead of what management had guided one quarter earlier [`01_management-and-track-record.md`, Section 4]; paying even part of one senior executive's package on revenue growth, in that specific context, points the same direction as the spending pattern already visible in the numbers rather than against it. Given the near-total absence of proxy disclosure, the honest classification is **"mixed"** — not because the visible evidence is balanced, but because there is too little of it to call outright misaligned, and what little exists (a revenue-based PSO metric, a large equity-heavy CFO package with no per-share performance gate, no say-on-pay data, no CEO disclosure at all) leans toward size rather than per-share value without proving a pattern.

Total insider ownership (Individuals/Insiders class, per the ownership-summary vendor export): **40.45% of total shares outstanding** (1,165,033,074 of 2,880,471,000 shares as of the position dates in the export, market value $178,576.3mm at the $145.48 close on Aug-12-2026) [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Public Ownership Summary.rtf, Ownership Summary table]. Ellison alone accounts for essentially all of it (40.21 of the 40.45 points). Institutions hold 44.01% (1,267,654,925 shares); Public and Other holds 15.40%.

**Bought vs. granted, in full.** Across the entire Form-4 history captured in the pool (2009–2026), neither Ellison nor Catz has a single **open-market cash purchase** on record. Ellison's share count has grown almost entirely through "Derivative Exercise and Retained Stock" transactions — he exercises vested stock options (paying the strike price in cash, e.g. $51.13/share on the July 2025 tranches) and keeps the resulting shares rather than selling them, which is a genuine cash outlay but is compensation-linked, not an open-market purchase decision made with disposable cash [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Public Ownership Insider Trading.xls, Ellison rows]. The handful of true open-market **buys** in the whole insider record belong to independent directors in small dollar amounts (e.g., Moorman IV, $947,913 in Feb-2025; Fairhead, $112,258 in Jul-2025) — none from the Executive Chair, the co-CEOs, or the CFO seat.

Aggregate trailing-12-month snapshot (per the vendor's own summary table, most recent 3-month slice): **May-13-2026 to Aug-13-2026 — 6 buy transactions totaling 12,546 shares vs. 3 sell transactions totaling 400,138 shares** [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Public Ownership Summary.rtf, Ownership Activity table]. Over the fuller 12-month window covered above (Aug-2025–Aug-2026), every transaction with a named senior executive (both co-CEOs, the outgoing bridge-CFO-turned-EVP, the Chief Accounting Officer, the Chief Legal Officer, and the Executive Vice Chairman) is a **sale** — either an open-market disposition or an option-exercise-and-immediate-sale. **No open-market purchases by any named executive officer or the Executive Chair are on record in the trailing 12 months.**

**Net insider activity: net selling.** Distinguishing the transaction types: the large-dollar Ellison and Catz transactions from the trailing period on record ($332mm and $307mm option exercises in July 2025, retained not sold) predate the strict 12-month window used here but establish the pattern — option exercises are typically either fully retained (building the founder stake further, funded by cash paid at strike) or exercised-and-sold in the same trade (monetizing, not accumulating). Within the strict trailing-12-month window, every dollar-material transaction by a named officer is a sale. The mechanical, same-day, price-laddered execution seen in Henley's, Sicilia's, and Levey's trades is consistent with pre-scheduled Rule 10b5-1 trading arrangements, which Oracle's insider trading policy explicitly permits for the Board and EVP-and-above tier [FY26 10-K, "Rule 10b5-1 Trading Plans"], but the pool's Form-4 export does not carry a field tagging which specific trades ran under a 10b5-1 plan — this is inferred from the pattern, not confirmed line-by-line, and is labeled accordingly.

**No pledging disclosed.** Oracle's own Insider Trading Policy, filed as an exhibit to the FY26 10-K, states: "the Pledging Policy prohibits applicable employees from holding Oracle securities in a margin account or otherwise pledging Oracle securities as collateral for a loan," with limited exceptions requiring Chief Legal Officer pre-approval [FY26 10-K, "Margin Accounts and Pledging Oracle Securities"]. This is a genuine, cited disclosure — not an inference from silence. The Ownership Summary, Ownership History, and Insider Trading workbooks in the pool contain zero mentions of pledged/encumbered shares for Ellison or any other insider [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Public Ownership Summary.rtf; Public Ownership History.xls; Public Ownership Insider Trading.xls]. Consistent with `business-model/01_disqualifier-scan.md`, which independently checked and cleared this item (computed ratio "not measurable / effectively 0%, well under the 50% threshold"). No RF-OWN-001/002 red flag is fired.

No shareholder agreement, standstill, or board-designation-rights provision for Ellison or any other holder was found in the 10-K or the ownership exports | [FY26 10-K; Public Ownership Summary.rtf] — absence of a provision, not independently confirmed against the proxy (DEF 14A not in the pool) |

This is the opposite profile of the three structurally-conflicted owner types the filter targets (government control, listed-subsidiary-of-a-parent, sprawling unrelated conglomerate) — a large founder stake concentrated in a single operating business is a classic alignment signal, not a structural cap | [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Public Ownership Summary.rtf]; [`management-governance/01_management-and-track-record.md`, Section 1] |

**Unaligned-owner test (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 6):** Does not apply. Oracle is not government-controlled, not a listed subsidiary of a value-maximizing parent, and not a sprawling unrelated-diversified conglomerate — it is a single-business operating company where the largest shareholder is the founder who built it and still runs product/technology strategy day to day (as CTO). **RF-OWN-004 is not triggered.** The relevant governance question for Oracle is not owner misalignment but the separate finding (already carried in `01_management-and-track-record.md`) that Ellison retains outsized influence (40.21% of the vote, plus the Chair and CTO seats) over a board and management team that also includes two non-founder co-CEOs — a founder-influence concentration risk, distinct from the §24 Filter 6 unaligned-owner test.

No trade-timing red flag is fired: the pool does not show insider selling immediately preceding a subsequently disclosed weak print, and the September 2025 and June 2026 sale clusters both sit around routine, publicly-known catalysts (a scheduled leadership transition and a scheduled earnings call) rather than ahead of undisclosed bad news. This is a negative finding (absence of the pattern), not an affirmative clearance — the pool does not include exchange-surveillance data that would independently confirm no unusual pre-announcement trading occurred.

## 5. Ownership / Insider Read

Insider skin in the game is real but almost entirely option-derived, not cash-bought on the open market: Ellison's 40.21% stake (worth roughly $168.5bn) grew through decades of exercise-and-retain option activity rather than a single disclosed open-market purchase, and no other named executive has bought shares with cash in the trailing 12 months either. The trailing-12-month insider signal is unambiguous net selling — every dollar-material Form 4 from the co-CEOs, the Executive Vice Chairman, the Chief Accounting Officer, and the Chief Legal Officer is a disposal, mechanically laddered in a way consistent with (but not confirmed as) pre-scheduled 10b5-1 plans, so this reads as routine liquidity monetization rather than a conviction signal in either direction. The biggest control-related fact for minority holders is Ellison's 40.21% vote concentrated with an active Executive Chair/CTO role sitting alongside a newly-installed non-founder co-CEO structure — not a pledging or encumbrance risk (pledging is company-policy-prohibited and none is disclosed), but a real concentration-of-influence factor to track once the 2026 proxy is available to confirm formal board-designation rights, if any.

# Board & Shareholder Rights — ORCL

## 0. Data Availability Note

Oracle's FY26 10-K incorporates Part III (Items 10–14: directors, executive compensation, security ownership, related-party transactions, and principal accountant fees) **entirely by reference** to the "2026 Proxy Statement," which the company states it will file with the SEC within 120 days of its May 31, 2026 fiscal year end [FY26 10-K, Part III, Items 10–14]. As of this report's date (2026-08-14), that 2026 proxy has not yet been filed, and no DEF 14A / proxy document of any vintage is in `data/ORCL/`. This is a genuine primary-source gap, not a language issue (CLAUDE.md §27) — the document simply does not exist yet for the current fiscal year.

Per the Partial-Data Rule, this agent used the pool's FY26 10-K signature page (which names the sitting board) and labeled, dated **web sources** — principally Oracle's most recently filed proxy (FY2025 DEF 14A, filed 2025-09-26, covering the board elected at the November 18, 2025 annual meeting) sourced via SEC EDGAR, Oracle's own bylaws/governance-guidelines filings, and the FY2025 annual-meeting voting-results 8-K — to fill governance facts not in the pool. These are CLAUDE.md §4 tier-7 web sources (search-engine syntheses of primary SEC filings, not a direct read of the filing text, since direct fetch of sec.gov returned HTTP 403). They are dated, labeled "Web (unverified)" throughout, and confidence is capped at 2–3 accordingly. Where a fact could not be found in any source, it is marked "Insufficient Data." The 2026 proxy, once filed, should be used to confirm or update every web-sourced fact below.

No lead independent director was identified in available sources — Insufficient Data on that specific point. | [FY26 10-K, Item 10 executive bios, "Mr. Ellison...has been our Executive Chair of the Board and Chief Technology Officer since September 2014"] |

Nominating/Governance committee's specific membership and independence were not confirmed from any available source — Insufficient Data on that slice. | [Web: Oracle FY2025 DEF 14A (filed 2025-09-26, sec.gov), search synthesis, 2026-08-14 (unverified) — "all directors who served during fiscal 2025 on the Compensation and F&A Committees were independent under the applicable NYSE and SEC heightened independence standards"] |

This is genuine refreshment, but it sits alongside — not in place of — the two 29–32-year tenures, and alongside two former CEOs (Catz, Henley) being retained on the board as Executive Vice Chairs rather than departing, which further concentrates insider continuity at the top of the board. | [Web: Oracle investor-relations press releases, "Oracle Names Stephen Rusckowski to the Board of Directors" and Mihaljevic election announcement, 2026-08-14 (unverified, dated)]; [FY26 10-K, Item 10] |

## 3. Related-Party Transactions & Group Leakage

| RPT Type | Amount | % of Revenue | % of PAT | % of Net Worth | Arm's Length? | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Sales to / purchases from related parties | Not disclosed | — | — | — | Not disclosed | [FY26 10-K, Related Party Disclosures note] |
| Loans / advances / guarantees to related parties | Not disclosed | — | — | — | Not disclosed | [FY26 10-K, Related Party Disclosures note] |
| Royalty / brand / management fees to founder/insider group | None disclosed | — | — | — | N/A | [FY26 10-K, Related Party Disclosures note] |
| Rent / other payments to insider-linked entities | None disclosed | — | — | — | N/A | [FY26 10-K, Related Party Disclosures note] |
| Outstanding receivables from related parties | Not disclosed | — | — | — | Not disclosed | [FY26 10-K, Related Party Disclosures note] |

**No material related-party transactions are disclosed for the current period.** The only related-party note in the audited FY26 10-K identifies equity-method investees (e.g., Ampere Computing, sold to SoftBank Nov-25-2025) as related parties under ASC 850, with no dollar transaction amounts attached — consistent with `business-model/01_disqualifier-scan.md`'s finding that RPTs do not trigger the >25%-of-revenue/expense hard disqualifier. Item 13 ("Certain Relationships and Related Transactions, and Director Independence") — the section that would carry any current-period insider-linked commercial dealings — is incorporated by reference to the unfiled 2026 proxy and cannot be checked directly (see Section 0).

**Historical precedent — the channel is not hypothetical.** Oracle's $9.3bn acquisition of NetSuite Inc. (closed FY17) was litigated for eight years as a related-party self-dealing claim: two derivative suits (filed May and July 2017, consolidated) alleged Ellison and Catz caused Oracle to overpay for NetSuite — a company in which Ellison personally held a large stake — effectively bailing out Ellison's own investment at Oracle shareholders' expense. The Delaware Court of Chancery's post-trial opinion (May 12, 2023) found the evidence fell "well short of proving" Ellison was a conflicted controller in the deal, and the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed that ruling on January 21, 2025 [Web: Dechert LLP case summary and Sidley "Enhanced Scrutiny" case note, both citing the Delaware Court of Chancery post-trial opinion and Delaware Supreme Court affirmance, 2026-08-14 (unverified, but citing primary court opinions)]. This is not a currently open red flag — it was fully litigated and resolved in the company's favor — but it is direct evidence that the founder/board self-dealing channel this section tests for is a real, previously-tested risk at Oracle, not a theoretical one, and that Ellison's ~40% stake plus board presence creates recurring exposure to this class of claim in future large acquisitions.

**Follow-up:** Once the 2026 proxy is filed, check Item 13 for any current insider-linked commercial contracts, family-member employment disclosures, or transactions with entities in which Ellison, Catz, or Henley hold an interest.

Oracle's Corporate Governance Guidelines add a majority-vote-and-resignation policy: in an uncontested election, a nominee who receives more "withheld" votes than "for" votes must tender a resignation, which the Board then has discretion to accept or reject. This is a softer standard than a true majority-vote requirement (where a nominee failing to win a majority is automatically not elected). | [Web: Oracle Amended and Restated Bylaws and Corporate Governance Guidelines, search synthesis, 2026-08-14 (unverified)] |
| Shareholder ability to call meetings / act by written consent | Call special meeting: yes, at a 20% ownership threshold. Written consent: not confirmed. | Shareholders holding ≥20% of outstanding common stock may call a special meeting. A 2015-era shareholder proposal sought to lower this threshold to 10%; available sources do not show it succeeded, so the 20% threshold appears to remain current — this should be re-verified against the 2026 proxy. No confirmed right to act by written consent in lieu of a meeting was found in any source (Insufficient Data — typical for Delaware companies with a special-meeting right to separately restrict written consent, but this is not confirmed and should not be assumed). | [Web: search synthesis of Oracle bylaws and a historical shareholder proposal, 2026-08-14 (unverified)] |

FY2024 Annual Meeting: ~78% for / ~22% against (i.e., worse than FY2025). Both years sit well below the >90% support typical of large-cap say-on-pay votes. | [Web: Oracle 8-K, FY2025 annual-meeting voting results, sec.gov, filed on/around 2025-11-21, search synthesis, 2026-08-14 (unverified)] |

The multi-year pattern of 18–22% opposition is consistent with, but does not prove, historical proxy-advisor concern about Oracle's pay design; treat this link as **Inference, not from filings**. | Insufficient Data (direct recommendation text not retrieved) |

The 18–22% opposition on say-on-pay over two consecutive annual meetings, while below the module's illustrative >20% single-year trigger in one of the two years and above it in the other, is a persistent, multi-year signal, not a one-off — flagged per RF-SHR-001.

## 5. Minority-Shareholder Protection Read

Board mechanics look reasonable on paper — single class of stock, annual (not staggered) director elections, a nominal 61.5% independent majority, and fully independent Audit and Compensation Committees — but the substance underneath is weaker: the board's own leadership seats concentrate insiders (Ellison as Executive Chair *and* CTO with ~40% of the vote, plus two former CEOs — Catz and Henley — retained as Executive Vice Chairs, plus both sitting co-CEOs), the director-election standard is plurality-with-discretionary-resignation rather than true majority voting, and two of the eight "independent" directors have sat on the board for 29–32 years alongside the founder they are meant to oversee. Say-on-pay opposition of 18–22% in each of the last two annual meetings is a real, recurring minority-shareholder signal that a meaningful bloc of outside investors is not satisfied with pay governance, even though it has never crossed the threshold needed to force a binding change. The single biggest self-dealing risk to minority holders is the founder-insider concentration on the board itself (Ellison/Catz/Henley/Magouyrk/Sicilia hold 5 of 13 seats, and Ellison alone controls ~40% of the vote) combined with a director-election standard that gives a dissatisfied minority no reliable mechanism to remove an entrenched nominee — a structure already tested once, in the NetSuite litigation, and resolved in the company's favor only after eight years of court proceedings. Governance and ownership disclosure for the *current* period is also incomplete because the 2026 proxy (which would carry Item 13's related-party detail and updated committee/voting facts) had not yet been filed as of this report's date. Verdict: **weak / entrenched**, primarily on structure (insider board seats + weak voting standard + long-tenured independents around the founder) rather than on any proven current-period self-dealing.

# Candor & Disclosure Quality — ORCL

All figures in USD unless stated otherwise. Fiscal year ends May 31 ("FY2026" = year ended May-31-2026). Reporting standard: US GAAP. This report draws on `01_management-and-track-record.md`, `earnings/06_earnings-quality.md`, and `earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md`, plus its own read of the FY2026 10-K and two verbatim earnings-call transcripts in the data pool.

**Transcript coverage caveat (governs Sections 1 and 4).** The data pool holds two verbatim earnings-call transcripts: FQ3 FY2026 (Mar 10, 2026) and FQ4 FY2026 (Jun 10, 2026) [Oracle Corporation, Q3 2026 Earnings Call, Mar 10, 2026.rtf; Oracle Corporation, Q4 2026 Earnings Call, Jun 10, 2026.rtf]. Both are quarters Oracle beat on revenue and EPS. The pool does **not** contain the FQ2 FY2026 (Dec 10, 2025) call transcript — the single worst quarter in the review period, where Oracle missed revenue, disclosed a $15 billion capex-guidance overshoot, and the stock fell 10.8% in a day [`01_management-and-track-record.md`, Section 4; Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Key Developments.xls, 2026-02-05 entry]. A law-firm press release quoting the Dec 10, 2025 earnings release ("now expect[ed] fiscal 2026 CapEx will be about $15 billion higher than [it] forecasted after Q1") is in the pool and is used below strictly for **what was disclosed** (the quantified fact), never for **how it was said** — no paraphrase or press release substitutes for a verbatim transcript on tone or Q&A-evasiveness (per this module's partial-data rule). Tone and Q&A directness in the actual crisis quarter are therefore marked **Insufficient Data** below, and the two available transcripts are used only to test general Q&A style in favorable quarters — a lower and different bar than "candor in bad times," and the two are not conflated.

## 1. Owning the Misses

| Miss (from 01) | How It Was Communicated | Owned or Obscured? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 capex guidance overshoot — management under-forecast capex by ~$15bn within one quarter | Company itself disclosed a specific, dated dollar figure in the Dec 10, 2025 earnings release: it "now expect[ed] fiscal 2026 CapEx will be about $15 billion higher than [it] forecasted after Q1." No vague "headwinds" language was used for this disclosure — this search found zero uses of the word "headwind" anywhere in the two available transcripts or the FY2026 10-K. The number was quantified and released in the same cycle the overshoot became known, not delayed to a later filing | **Owned, on the numbers** — specific, dated, quantified. Tone during the actual Dec 10, 2025 Q&A (defensive vs. plain) is **Insufficient Data** — that transcript is not in the pool | [Oracle Corporation NYSE ORCL Key Developments.xls, 2026-02-05 entry, quoting the Dec 10, 2025 earnings release]; [`01_management-and-track-record.md`, Section 4] |
| FQ2 FY2026 EPS "beat" driven by one-time Ampere/Bloom Energy gains, not operating performance | Management's own FY2026 press release footnote states plainly: "Q4 and FY 2026 results include one-time net investment gains from certain transactions." On the Q4 FY26 call itself, CFO Maxson volunteered the ex-gains number without being asked: "Our non-GAAP EPS was up 27% in U.S. dollars to $7.63, including onetime gains on investment. Excluding these gains, our non-GAAP EPS was $6.83" — a 10.5-point gap she stated in her prepared remarks, not under analyst pressure | **Owned, proactively** — this is the strongest positive candor signal in the record: management named its own inflated number and gave the clean number unprompted | [Q4 FY26 transcript, CFO Maxson prepared remarks]; [`earnings/06_earnings-quality.md`, Section 4] |
| Gross margin compression (-469bps FY2026, guided to step down further in FY2027) | CFO Maxson stated directly on the Q4 call: "gross margin declining driven by impacts from ramping up our data centers and the acceleration in our infrastructure revenue," and for FY2027: it "will step down due to timing for the ramp-up of our data center projects into their full revenue contribution plus impacts from mix." The 10-K MD&A gives the same explanation in writing | **Owned, specific mechanism named** — not attributed to vague "market conditions" | [Q4 FY26 transcript, CFO Maxson]; [`earnings/03_margin-drivers.md`, Section 3] |
| Unresolved securities class action alleging Oracle overstated its AI-deal growth outlook (filed Feb 3, 2026; RF-MGT-005 in `01`) | Disclosed only as required, standard legal-proceedings boilerplate in the 10-K (Note 15): "We believe that we have meritorious defenses against this action, and we will continue to vigorously defend it... we do not believe that it will have a material impact." Neither of the two available earnings-call transcripts (Mar 10 or Jun 10, 2026) contains any analyst question or management comment addressing the substance of the allegation — that the AI-deal growth outlook itself was overstated | **Neither owned nor obscured in an active sense — simply not engaged.** Standard legal boilerplate satisfies disclosure requirements but does not amount to management addressing the substantive question live, which a genuinely candid team facing an outlook-integrity allegation might choose to do | [FY26 10-K, Note 15, "Legal Proceedings — Securities Class Action Regarding Oracle Cloud Infrastructure"]; [Q3 FY26 transcript]; [Q4 FY26 transcript] |
| Worst-quarter (FQ2 FY26) Q&A tone and directness | Not assessable — the Dec 10, 2025 call transcript is absent from the data pool | **Insufficient Data** — do not infer from the two adjacent good-quarter transcripts, which test a different (favorable-results) condition | — |

## 2. Non-GAAP / Adjustment Aggressiveness

| Signal | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Recurring "one-off" addbacks | Restructuring & other charges excluded from non-GAAP results recurred in consecutive fiscal years under successive named plans: 2024 Restructuring Plan ($374M, FY2025) and a newly initiated 2026 Restructuring Plan ($1,838M, FY2026). A charge labelled "restructuring" that recurs every year under a new plan name is the textbook recurring "one-off" — RF-DISC-002 triggered | earnings/06, Sections 4, 5, 8 |
| GAAP-to-adjusted gap (magnitude / trend) | Operating income gap: 40.4% of reported (FY2026) vs 41.6% (FY2025) — consistently large, not a one-year anomaly. Net income gap: 30.7% (FY2026) vs 38.9% (FY2025). Stock-based compensation alone ($4,811M, 28.2% of GAAP net income) drives over half of the total addback in both years, and is excluded from non-GAAP results in full every year | earnings/06, Section 7 |
| Does adjusted framing flatter reality? | Yes, on two specific dimensions the module's own scan already caught: (1) the GAAP effective tax rate (12.6%) sits well below the company's own non-GAAP rate (19.9%), a gap driven mainly by stock-based-compensation-related tax benefits that scale with the share price, not operating performance; (2) a $2,493M pre-tax Ampere Computing sale gain plus Bloom Energy warrant gains drove roughly a third of FY2026's reported 36% net-income-available-to-common growth. Management itself backs the investment gains out of its own forward growth math (18% vs. 34% headline non-GAAP EPS growth) — a genuine mitigating factor, since the flattering treatment is disclosed and self-corrected, not hidden | earnings/06, Sections 8, 10 |

**New metric introduced the same year capex ballooned.** Oracle introduced a company-defined "net cash outlay for capital expenditures" metric on the Q4 FY2026 call — $70bn guided for FY2027, versus a gross capex figure of $90–95bn once ~$20–25bn of customer prepayments and timing impacts are added back [Q4 FY26 transcript, CFO Maxson prepared remarks]. The netting is disclosed with a reconciliation (not hidden), and it tracks a real cash mechanic (large customer prepayments, which `earnings/06` independently verified are cash-backed, not fabricated). But introducing a new, smaller-looking headline capex number in the exact year gross capex nearly tripled ($21.2bn → $55.7bn) is a framing choice worth flagging, not a neutral change in convention.

## 3. Disclosure Transparency

Segment and operating disclosure is genuinely specific, not boilerplate: management discloses global GPU utilization (97.5%), a stated RPO-conversion schedule (12% recognized in the next 12 months, 34% in months 13–36), and site-by-site capacity-delivery percentages for its five largest data centers [Q4 FY26 transcript, CEO Magouyrk]. Results are filed 10 days after quarter-end — management calls this out itself as the fastest in the S&P 500 — and no delayed-filing or delayed-disclosure pattern was found in the pool (RF-REG-002 not triggered). Disclosure got LESS transparent in one specific respect worth watching: capex maintenance-vs-growth spend is not broken out (unchanged, a standing gap, not new), and the new "net cash outlay for capex" metric (Section 2) replaces gross capex as the headline figure precisely when gross capex became the least flattering number to lead with.

## 4. Tone in Bad Times

**Not directly assessable for the actual worst quarter** — the Dec 10, 2025 (FQ2 FY26) transcript, the quarter that missed revenue, disclosed the $15bn capex overshoot, and cost the stock 10.8%, is absent from the pool. What is assessable: the two available transcripts (both strong-beat quarters) show management answering hard, specific questions directly rather than deflecting — e.g., on the Q4 FY26 call, when analyst John DiFucci noted Oracle "spent a little bit more this quarter on CapEx than we expected" and asked about rising component costs, CEO Magouyrk gave a specific, technical answer (fixed-price vs. floating-price contract mechanics tied to cost certainty) rather than a generic reassurance. That is evidence of a generally non-evasive Q&A style, but it is evidence from favorable quarters and cannot stand in for how the team handled the actual bad print — "anyone is candid when results are good" is exactly the gap this report cannot close from the available pool.

## 5. Candor Read

Oracle's disclosure is specific and numbers-heavy where it counts — the $15bn capex miss, the ex-one-off EPS figure, and the gross-margin mechanism were each given a dated, quantified explanation rather than vague language, and the CFO volunteered the least flattering number ($6.83 ex-gains vs. $7.63 headline) unprompted on the Q4 call. Set against that: restructuring charges have recurred as "one-offs" under successive named plans for two straight years, the non-GAAP-to-GAAP gap has stayed above 40% of operating income for two years running, a new company-defined capex metric appeared the same quarter gross capex nearly tripled, and prepared-remarks language ("tremendous quarter," "overdelivering... across the board") describes a beat streak that `earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md` shows is closer to a coin flip (2 of 4 quarters clean on both revenue and EPS once one-off gains are stripped) — a real gap between the verbal framing and the underlying numbers. The single biggest candor signal is a genuine gap in the evidence, not a finding: the pool has no verbatim record of how management spoke in the one quarter that actually went badly, so this report cannot confirm candor was maintained under real pressure — only that the numbers, when disclosed, were disclosed specifically. Combined with the unresolved securities-fraud allegation (RF-MGT-005, routed from `01`) that management has not substantively addressed beyond legal boilerplate, this compounds rather than nets out against the positive specificity evidence. Verdict: **mixed**.

RF-DISC-002 (recurring "one-off" / aggressive non-GAAP add-backs)

RF-DISC-001 (commentary contradicting the numbers)

# Valuation Module — ORCL (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Oracle screens modestly overvalued: the triangulated base-case fair value is $133.77 a share, about 13% below the $153.94 price, so the margin of safety is negative — a cushion of roughly zero, not a small one. Bull, base and headline-bear levels of $212.67, $133.77 and $31.44 (a 24–36 month structural-reset bear, next to a milder $94.62 twelve-month cyclical trough) are anchored on own-history and peer multiples, with the intrinsic DCF corroborating caution. The reverse-DCF shows today's price already assumes a 51% FY2027 revenue beat against management's own 33.6% guide and a 62% terminal margin no peer has ever reached — aggressive, bordering on unachievable. The real downside anchor is the structural bear case, a 79.6% fall, tied to Oracle's 4.46x net-debt-to-EBITDA leverage and an eroding return on capital funding a concentrated AI-infrastructure bet. Net: fairly-to-modestly rich, not a bargain.

## 1. Valuation Verdict

- **Verdict:** Modestly overvalued
- **Base-case fair value (point, per share):** $133.77
- **Current price:** $153.94 (Aug-13-2026, 02:26 PM GMT-5, delayed NYSE quote, Capital IQ pool export; price-state `pool-verified`, 1 trading day old)
- **Bull / Base / Bear fair-value levels (points):** Bull $212.67 (+38.2% vs price) / Base $133.77 (−13.1% vs price) / Bear-cyclical $94.62 (12-month trough, −38.5% vs price) / Bear-structural (headline) $31.44 (24–36 month reset, −79.6% vs price)
- **Cross-method dispersion (football field, low–high):** $68.92 (intrinsic DCF, Gordon terminal) to $212.01 (raw SOTP peer-parity ceiling) — a 207.7% high-to-low spread; the three weighted methods alone span $68.92–$151.27
- Valuation attractiveness /100 (higher = cheaper): **25** — base fair value sits below price; no discount to unlock
- Margin of safety /100 (higher = better): **15** — margin of safety is **−15.08%** (negative; price trades above base-case fair value, so there is no cushion)
- Valuation confidence /100: **55** — capped at 60 by the terminal-value dominance rule (DCF terminal value = 80.7% of EV, MODULE_RULES Score-Cap row); set below the cap given the 208% cross-method spread
- Downside risk /100 (higher = worse, inverted): **85** — downside-to-bear (headline, structural) is **79.58%**; even the milder 12-month cyclical-trough bear implies 38.5%
- Data quality /100: **90** — full filings, consensus (41 analysts), a 10-name peer comp set, and complete capital-structure data; `00_valuation-data-triage.md` verdicts "Sufficient," no critical gaps
- Overall usefulness /100: **85**
- Dominant valuation method (one line): own-history (`02`) and peer (`03`) multiples anchor the base (80% combined weight, per the multiples-first policy), with intrinsic DCF (`04`, 20%) trusted as a genuine corroborating cross-check rather than an outlier — three independent lenses (DCF, reverse-DCF, and the business-model module's eroding-moat finding) converge on the same caution
- What's priced in (one line): a 51.3% FY2027 revenue beat against management's own +33.6% guide, a 22.6% revenue CAGR through FY2034, and a 61.9% terminal EBIT margin with no peer precedent (best peer: Microsoft 46.8%) — aggressive, bordering on unachievable
- Biggest valuation risk (one line): Oracle carries net debt/EBITDA of 4.46x and generated −$23.7bn of free cash flow in FY26 funding a concentrated, four-mega-customer AI-infrastructure bet; if that RPO backlog ($638bn, +363% YoY) fails to convert to margin-protected cash on schedule, both the DCF and the structural-reset bear case say the downside is severe, not shallow

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** the reverse-DCF (`05`) shows today's price requires expectations with no historical or peer precedent — a 51.3% FY2027 revenue beat vs. management's own just-issued +33.6% guide, and a 61.9% terminal EBIT margin (best peer, Microsoft, is 46.8%) — while the intrinsic DCF's own base case (`04`) sits 55.2% below price and the business-model module independently verdicts the moat "eroding" (ROIC 12.35%→8.22% over four years, now at/below the ~11.2% estimated WACC).
- **Strongest bull point (steelman):** the two methods actually anchored on what the market pays — own-history (`02`, $151.27) and peer multiples (`03`, $148.70) — land within 2 points of each other and close to today's price, despite being built from entirely independent data; Oracle's PEG ratio (0.65) is roughly half the peer median (1.31), and the raw SOTP peer-parity ceiling ($212.01) shows real optionality if the $638bn RPO backlog converts to cash the way management projects.
- **Single killer risk specific to the fair-value read:** AI-infrastructure customer concentration — `earnings/07_earnings-sensitivity.md` ranks this the #1 sensitivity, with a modeled downside of −$6,937M EBITDA (23% of FY26 EBITDA) if one of the four >$8bn named customers pulls back, and "no disclosed upside mirror of comparable size." This single variable is the fulcrum between the $212.67 bull and the $31.44–$94.62 bear range.
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** `05`'s independent market-ceiling check converts the price-implied FY2030 revenue into an implied global cloud-infrastructure market share of ≈14–17% (vs. ≈3% today) — a 5–6x share gain in four years that no hyperscaler (AWS, Azure) has ever achieved this fast. This is a second, independent kill signal pointing the same direction as the terminal-margin finding, not a reason to soften the read.

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| price-and-capital-structure | Price-state `pool-verified`, $153.94, 1 day old | EV $584,464.2M (lease-inclusive); net debt (strict) $136,143M; tangible book value is **negative** (−$9.70/share) on $65.5bn of goodwill/intangibles |
| multiples-own-history | Oracle trades close to its own 5-year median on EV-based multiples (17–32nd percentile), not a statistical extreme | Own-median EV/EBIT reversion implies ~$151.27/share — essentially flat to price — but that "in line with history" read sits on top of net debt that rose 38.7% YoY |
| relative-valuation-peers | Neither clearly cheap nor expensive — the answer flips depending on which peer slice is used | Quality-adjusted base case (leverage- and moat-adjusted 11.5x NTM EV/EBITDA) is $148.70/share (−3.4%); raw peer-median dispersion runs $118.10–$191.75 |

## 3. Reconciliation

The high-to-low spread across methods is **207.7%** ($68.92 DCF to $212.01 raw SOTP), well above the 40% Reconciliation-Gate tolerance — this spread is the single biggest finding of this module and is led with, not averaged away. Two clusters exist: (1) the multiples methods — own-history ($151.27) and peers ($148.70) — land within 2 points of each other despite independent data sources, and both sit close to today's price; (2) the DCF ($68.92) sits 119.5% below that cluster. `07_scenario-and-fair-value.md` does not treat the DCF's low reading as a stray outlier to discount to zero: it is corroborated by two other independent lenses in the same run — the reverse-DCF's finding that price already requires precedent-free growth and margin assumptions, and the business-model module's independently-derived "eroding" moat verdict (return on capital below cost of capital for four straight years). Because three independent methods point the same direction, the DCF is weighted at 20% (not zero, not equal-weighted to the multiples methods) per the multiples-first policy, pulling the blended base ($133.77) below both multiples methods individually — a disclosed, reasoned departure from a pure 02/03 average (~$150.0), not a silent drag. The raw SOTP ($212.01) is excluded from the blend entirely because `06` itself states its base case is a "peer-parity ceiling," not a base fair value, since it implicitly prices Oracle's leverage (net debt/EBITDA 4.46x) as if it were MSFT's (0.6x) or SAP's (0.8x). **Trust ranking for this company: own-history and peer multiples for the central tendency; DCF and reverse-DCF as the disciplining cross-check on whether that central tendency is achievable; raw SOTP as an optimistic ceiling only.**

## 4. Score Cap Application

| Cap Trigger | Applied? (Y/N) | Affected Score | Final Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| No pool-verified price (price-state `indicative` or `none`) | N — price is `pool-verified`, 1 trading day old | — | Not applicable |
| No consensus / forward estimates | N — 41-analyst consensus present | — | Not applicable |
| No peer data | N — 10-name Capital IQ comp set present | — | Not applicable |
| Only one valuation method usable | N — five methods ran (02, 03, 04, 05, 06) | — | Not applicable |
| No cash flow AND DCF is only method | N — cash flow statement present; multiples also run | — | Not applicable |
| SOTP not possible for multi-segment | N — SOTP ran and collapsed to single-segment per its own data-driven finding, not a missing-data block | — | Not applicable |
| Methods disagree >40% unreconciled | N — spread is 207.7% but `07` explicitly reconciled it (three-lens corroboration for the DCF's low reading, §3 above); not a silent average | — | Not applicable |
| Terminal value >75% of DCF EV | **Y** — DCF terminal value is 80.7% of EV (`04` §5a) | Valuation confidence | **Max 60** (set at 55, below the cap, given the added 207.7% cross-method spread) |
| Misaligned controlling owner (RF-OWN-004) | N — founder Larry Ellison (40.21% of vote) is an engaged, value-aligned Executive Chair/CTO, not a value-indifferent controller; `management-governance/99` finding 04-008 confirms the filter does not trip | — | Not applicable |

## 5. Fair-Value Summary

The bull ($212.67), base ($133.77), and headline-bear ($31.44) levels are driven by two different logics: bull and base are built off own-history and peer NTM/FY2027 EV/EBITDA multiples (14.0x expanding case, ~10.63x implied base), while the headline bear is a declining-perpetuity DCF reset (terminal margin 22.0%, below Oracle's own FY23 trough, terminal ROIC 7.0%, below WACC) rather than a metric-times-multiple construction — the correct method for an operating-company permanent-impairment scenario. The current $153.94 price implies, per the reverse-DCF, a 51.3% FY2027 revenue beat against management's own freshly-issued +33.6% guide and a 61.9% terminal EBIT margin with no peer precedent; earnings-module evidence does not support this — Oracle's own 4-year revenue CAGR is 12.2%, and the #1 named earnings sensitivity (AI-customer concentration) points toward downside, not upside, of comparable size. The margin of safety is **−15.08%** (price sits above, not below, base-case fair value — no cushion), a separate and distinct read from the downside-to-bear, which is **79.58%** to the headline structural-reset case (or 38.54% to the milder 12-month cyclical trough). This is not a classic value-trap setup — no misaligned controlling owner, and the moat is genuinely eroding rather than being unfairly discounted — but the mirror image of one: the stock is priced for the optimistic scenario (RPO backlog converting cleanly to margin-protected cash) while carrying leverage (net debt/EBITDA 4.46x) and cash-flow evidence (−$23.7bn FY26 FCF) that argue for caution, not a premium.

## 6. What Would Change The Valuation Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Make It Cheaper | What Would Make It More Expensive | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Modestly overvalued | Price falls toward or below $133.77 (base FV) without a fair-value deterioration; OR the FY2027 print lands at or above the guided +33.6% with gross margin recovering per management's "improves rapidly" claim, which would lift the multiples-methods base and narrow the DCF-vs-multiples gap | The stock re-rates further above $153.94 on continued AI-infrastructure enthusiasm with no confirming margin/cash-flow evidence; OR one of the four >$8bn named customers cuts contracted RPO (the #1 named earnings sensitivity), pulling the multiples-methods base down toward the DCF's $68.92 | The FY2027 actual print (revenue growth and gross margin, due within the fiscal year ending May-2027) — the single nearest-term, most falsifiable test of what today's price already assumes; a historical peer-premium/discount panel (currently "Not assessable" per `03` §3) would sharpen whether the relative-valuation read is typical or unusual |

## 7. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- Bull/base/bear fair-value levels: **$212.67 / $133.77 / $31.44** (headline, 24–36mo structural reset) — a milder 12-month cyclical-trough bear also exists at **$94.62**, kept as a separate, fully-computed case (not merged into the headline). Dominant method: own-history + peer multiples (80% combined weight) for the central tendency, with intrinsic DCF (20%) disciplining it downward on corroborated, not cherry-picked, grounds.
- What the price implies (from reverse-DCF): a 51.3% FY2027 revenue beat vs. management's own +33.6% guide, a 22.6% revenue CAGR through FY2034, and a 61.9% terminal EBIT margin with no peer precedent — earnings-module evidence (12.2% historical 4-year CAGR; AI-customer concentration as the #1 downside sensitivity) does not support this being achievable.
- Margin of safety is **−15.08%** (no cushion — price above base fair value) and downside-to-bear is **79.58%** (headline structural) / **38.54%** (cyclical-trough context) — these are two distinct numbers, not one collapsed metric.
- This is genuine caution, not a value trap: no misaligned controlling owner trips (§24 Filter 6 does not apply — Ellison is engaged and value-aligned), and the moat is independently verdicted "eroding" by the business-model module (ROIC below WACC, 4 straight years), so the warranted multiple is not a premium one — the current price is closer to requiring a re-rating the fundamentals have not yet earned than to reflecting an unfair discount.
- Trust own-history (`02`) and peer (`03`) multiples for the central tendency on this company; trust the DCF (`04`) and reverse-DCF (`05`) as the disciplining cross-check on achievability, not as a stray low outlier; discount the raw SOTP (`06`, $212.01) to a ceiling reference only — it prices Oracle's balance sheet as if it were MSFT's or SAP's, which it is not.
- No partial-data cap applied for missing price/consensus/peers — data is complete. The one cap that DID apply: terminal value is 80.7% of DCF EV, capping valuation confidence at 60 (set at 55 here, reflecting the added 207.7% cross-method dispersion).
- Biggest missing data point (single highest-value next request): a multi-year historical peer-premium/discount panel for the CIQ comp set — `03` could only source a single-date (2026-08-13) snapshot, so whether ORCL's current premium/discount to peers is typical or unusual for THIS stock cannot be assessed; this would sharpen the relative-valuation read materially.
- **Explicit handoff:** the master synthesizer's "Valuation and Peer Mispricing" section should defer to this synthesis. The bull/base/bear fair-value LEVELS here ($212.67 / $133.77 / $31.44, plus the $94.62 cyclical-trough context case) are the inputs for the master's probability-weighted scenario model — this module assigns no probabilities.

## 8. Simple Summary

- Oracle is **modestly overvalued**, not cheap: base fair value is $133.77 against a $153.94 price, about 13% rich.
- Bull / base / bear levels: **$212.67 / $133.77 / $31.44** (headline structural-reset bear, 24–36 months out); a milder 12-month cyclical-trough bear sits at $94.62.
- The market is pricing in a 51% beat of Oracle's own just-issued FY2027 growth guidance and a profit margin no software peer has ever reached — an aggressive, largely unproven bet.
- The real downside is severe if that bet fails: **79.6%** to the structural-reset bear case, tied to Oracle's heavy debt load (4.46x net debt/EBITDA) and negative free cash flow (−$23.7bn in FY26) funding a concentrated AI-infrastructure build.
- Own-history and peer trading multiples matter most for this stock — they anchor the fair-value estimate; the discounted-cash-flow model is the disciplining cross-check, not the headline.
- This is not a classic value trap (no misaligned controlling owner) — it is closer to the opposite: the stock is priced for a best-case outcome while its own moat is independently found to be eroding.
- A current, verified price was available throughout — no data gap on that front; the module's data quality is high (90/100).
- This module is highly useful for the master synthesizer: it delivers concrete, reconciled fair-value levels, a clear "what's priced in" read, and a named killer risk (AI-customer concentration) that ties the bull and bear cases together.

| Own-history multiples | Y | None | 10-year own-history multiple series available (`Financials_Annual.xls` / `Financials_Quarterly.xls`, Multiples tabs) |
| Peer relative valuation | Y | None | 10 named peers, LTM and NTM multiples, as of 2026-08-13 |
| Intrinsic DCF (Operating FCFF) | Y | None | Income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement all present; FY2026 reported FCF is negative on heavy AI-infrastructure capex — `04` must build a normalized FCF base and flag the capex cycle rather than average it into a steady-state figure (CLAUDE.md §15) |
| Reverse DCF | Y (conditional on `04` running first) | None from this triage's read; depends on `04`'s canonical WACC and normalized FCF base per MODULE_RULES Calculation Standard 9 | Pool-verified price present, so "what's priced in" is computable |
| SOTP | Y (data present), but expected to collapse | None — three segments disclosed, but Cloud and Software is 86.9% of revenue / 90.7% of segment profit in FY26, above the module's >85%-of-EBIT single-segment threshold | `06` should return the "single-segment — SOTP collapses to the consolidated read" note per the Segment/SOTP Rule rather than force a breakup; this is a business-mix finding, not a missing-data gap |

## 6. Sufficiency Verdict

- **Verdict:** Sufficient
- **Reason:** A complete earnings base (income statement and cash flow statement), full capital-structure data (balance sheet, debt, cash, preferred, minority interest), a pool-verified current price, consensus forward estimates, and a named peer-comps export are all present in the data pool, so all five candidate methods (own-history multiples, peer relative valuation, DCF, reverse-DCF, and SOTP) can run.
- **Methods that can run:** own-history multiples, peer relative valuation, intrinsic DCF (Operating FCFF), reverse-DCF, SOTP (though SOTP is expected to collapse to a single-segment note given Cloud and Software's 90.7% share of FY26 segment profit).
- **Active partial-data caps:** None — no Partial-Data Rule row is triggered.
- **Critical missing items:** None. Two items merit explicit handling downstream, not as data gaps: (1) FY2026 reported free cash flow is negative (~ -$23.7bn) due to an AI data-center capex surge — `04_intrinsic-dcf` must build a normalized FCF base and flag the capex cycle explicitly rather than headline the negative figure or silently smooth it away; (2) Cloud and Software is 90.7% of FY26 segment profit, so `06_sum-of-the-parts` should apply the module's single-segment collapse note rather than force a three-way breakup.
